Mastering: Identifies the Wheeling speech (February 1950) and gives specific detail, e.g. McCarthy claimed to hold a list of 205 Communists working in the State Department, though the number varied between speeches. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to McCarthy making accusations. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the methods McCarthy used during his anti-Communist campaign.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) McCarthy made sweeping accusations without verifiable evidence, shifting his claims when challenged; (2) he labelled critics as Communist sympathisers, making it dangerous to oppose him publicly. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why McCarthyism attracted support from different groups in American society in the early 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains support from multiple groups with specific evidence — Republican politicians used anti-Communism to attack Democrats; business conservatives saw it as a weapon against New Deal liberalism; religious groups feared atheist Communism; ordinary Americans were frightened by genuine external threats. Shows how these groups' motivations reinforced each other. Secure: Two or more reasons explained with evidence. Developing: Lists groups without explaining their motivations. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why opposition to McCarthyism grew between 1950 and 1954.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) Edward R. Murrow's 1954 television broadcasts exposed McCarthy's methods to a mass audience, shifting public opinion against him; (2) the Army-McCarthy hearings, broadcast live on television, allowed millions to see McCarthy's bullying style and hear Welch's rebuke, making his support unsustainable. Each reason includes specific evidence and a clear explanation. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence and explanation. Developing: Two reasons identified but limited development. Emerging: One weak reason.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of television in ending McCarthy's political career?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis weighing television against other factors. Television was significant: Murrow's programmes and the live Army-McCarthy hearings let millions judge McCarthy directly; the medium showed his methods rather than just reporting them. But other factors also matter: the Army's willingness to fight back provided the forum; McCarthy's overreach (attacking the Army) alienated Republican allies; the Tydings Committee report and growing Senate opposition existed independently. Integrated judgement about relative significance. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes television's role without weighing it against other factors. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the causes and effects of McCarthyism on American society in the years 1950 to 1954.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering causes (external shocks, political opportunism, genuine fear, institutional mechanisms) and effects (careers destroyed, civil liberties eroded, chilling effect on free speech, political opponents silenced) with well-chosen evidence throughout. Reaches an integrated judgement. Secure: Several causes and effects with evidence; some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited analytical structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways castles helped William I control England after 1066.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise feature with accurate supporting detail (e.g. motte-and-bailey castles could be built quickly using forced labour, allowing rapid establishment of Norman garrisons). Developing: vague (e.g. 'they were strong buildings').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the feudal system introduced by the Normans.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for accurate supporting detail). Mastering: e.g. king grants land to tenants-in-chief in exchange for knight service; barons sublet to knights in exchange for military obligation. Developing: identifies features without supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Harrying of the North (1069–70) was significant in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links military effectiveness (destroyed northern resistance), economic impact (Domesday evidence of 'waste'), and psychological deterrence (future risings suppressed by example). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence — explains significance with accurate detail across two or more reasons. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence. Emerging: Simple points; evidence limited or missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the feudal system sometimes broke down in the period 1066–1215.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers disputed succession (The Anarchy 1135), weak king unable to enforce obligations (John), and how barons exploited weakness for their own gain; links to Magna Carta as outcome. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Norman Conquest change the lives of ordinary people in England? Explain your answer using evidence from the period 1066–1215.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — balanced essay covering changed lives (Harrying, castle construction destroying homes, villeinage, replacement of Anglo-Saxon lords) and elements of continuity (farming patterns, basic village structure, Christian church) with a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence and sustained explanation. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence, mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Magna Carta (1215) was an important consequence of the breakdown of the feudal relationship between king and barons.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links John's specific violations of feudal compact (scutage, arbitrary fines, loss of Normandy), explains how this motivated barons to act collectively, and analyses Magna Carta's significance as a limit on royal power. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the 1950 Marriage Law.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the law and provides a specific supported detail (e.g. what it banned or the right it granted women). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but lacking specific detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Communist social policies towards education under Mao.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise detail (e.g. literacy campaigns, restructuring on Soviet model, political curriculum). Secure: Two features, each with some detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack supporting evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the CCP's social policies towards women had a limited impact in rural areas.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons with specific evidence (e.g. inconsistent cadre enforcement, rural traditional attitudes, hukou restrictions), linking causes. Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1950 Marriage Law for women in China.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis across criteria (immediate legal impact, urban vs rural variation, longer-term effects); counter-argument considered. Secure: Clear argument about significance with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis of why significant. Emerging: Describes the law with minimal argument about significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did Communist social policies under Mao represent a break from Chinese traditionalism? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence of both change (Marriage Law, literacy, iron rice bowl) and continuity (rural enforcement gaps, Confucian attitudes persisting, state patriarchy); balanced and well-evidenced. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from multiple policy areas; some weighing of change vs continuity. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the CCP placed political education at the centre of the school curriculum under Mao.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons with specific evidence (e.g. need to build loyalty, break with Confucian tradition, prepare industrial workforce). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways the indenture system suited the Hundred Years' War better than the feudal levy.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. paid soldiers could serve for the full duration of a campaign in France, unlike feudal levies who were only obligated for forty days per year). Developing: vague (e.g. 'it was more reliable').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Edward I's approach to controlling Wales after 1277.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. construction of concentric castles such as Caernarfon and Harlech as garrison points; military campaigns in 1277 and 1282–83 that crushed Welsh resistance. Developing: identifies features without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Agincourt (1415) was significant for the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers tactical factors (terrain, longbow deployment), political consequences (Treaty of Troyes 1420, Henry V named heir to France), and longer-term context (English military prestige, subsequent loss of France). Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Hundred Years' War was financially damaging for both England and France.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers cost of paid armies, Parliamentary taxation, chevauchée destroying French tax revenue, impact on wool trade and civilian populations. Secure: Clear argument with two reasons explained with accurate evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the nature of warfare change between c.1290 and c.1450? Explain your answer with examples from Edward I's campaigns and the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — balanced essay covering change (feudal levy to indenture, longbow replacing mounted knight as battle-winner, castle design from motte-and-bailey to concentric) and continuity (chivalric ideals, role of cavalry, siege warfare) with a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument, mostly change or continuity only. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Scottish Wars of Independence were significant in shaping Edward I's military reputation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains initial success (1296 deposition of Balliol, conquest of castles), then long-term failure (Wallace, Bruce, Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton 1328), and analyses how this mixed legacy affected his reputation as 'Hammer of the Scots'. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Massacre of Glencoe (1692) shocked Scotland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. Campbell soldiers killed their MacDonald hosts after two weeks of Highland hospitality; a parliamentary inquiry called it murder under trust, yet nobody was prosecuted). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Darien Scheme (1698–1700) failed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. disease, Spanish attack and lack of supplies destroyed the colony; William III refused naval help and warned English and Dutch colonies not to assist the Scots). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Darien Scheme's failure helped bring about the Act of Union in 1707.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking Darien's financial devastation to Scotland's economic weakness, England's colonial blocking, and the mutual strategic incentives for union, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one causal link explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: 'Scotland gained more than it lost from the Act of Union of 1707.' How far do you agree? Use Sources A and B [supplied in the exam] and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs both sides, uses precise evidence (access to English colonial trade and financial stability against the loss of the Scottish Parliament, the bribery claims and the rising of 1715), works both sources into the argument, and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence and some use of the sources. Developing: Some argument; sources described rather than used. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence. Five of the 25 marks are for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Massacre of Glencoe (1692) damaged William III's reputation in Scotland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the orders traced back to William or his government, the violation of Highland hospitality ('murder under trust'), and the parliamentary condemnation without prosecution. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Explain what changed in Scotland because of the Act of Union (1707).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed changes with precise evidence (e.g. the Scottish Parliament was abolished and Scottish members went to Westminster; Scotland gained access to English colonial trade while keeping its Kirk, law and universities). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one change. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Dawes Plan of 1924.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Feature 1: Rescheduled German reparations payments to match economic capacity (1); removed the immediate cause of Franco-German conflict over the Ruhr (1). Feature 2: Secured US loans to Germany at commercial rates (1); created a circular flow of US capital enabling Germany to pay reparations to France and Britain (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Locarno Treaties of 1925 were seen as a major step towards European stability.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed — Germany voluntarily accepted the Rhineland demilitarisation and western borders (showing genuine commitment rather than coerced acceptance); the spirit of co-operation led to German admission to the League in 1926, integrating Germany into the international system for the first time since Versailles. Secure: Both explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained, one named. Emerging: General reference to peace without specific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and up to 2 marks for specific supporting detail. Feature 1: Signed by 62 nations (1); making it one of the most widely subscribed diplomatic agreements of the interwar period (1). Feature 2: Signatory states renounced war as an instrument of national policy (1); but the pact had no enforcement mechanism to punish states that violated it (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the international agreements of the 1920s failed to provide lasting European stability.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Multiple interlocking causes explained — over-dependence on US investment (Dawes Plan circular flow collapsed with Wall Street Crash); Locarno did not cover eastern borders, leaving German revisionism towards Poland unresolved; Kellogg-Briand lacked enforcement; disarmament conference failed; German nationalists never accepted the post-war settlement as legitimate. Connects causes to show systemic fragility. Secure: Two or more causes explained. Developing: One cause explained, others listed. Emerging: General statement without causal analysis.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of the 1920s international agreements. Interpretation A argues they represented genuine progress towards a stable European order. Interpretation B sees them as a fragile facade concealing unresolved post-war tensions. How far do these interpretations differ and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies substantive differences (what each counts as evidence of stability or instability); uses own knowledge (Locarno's eastern-border gap, Kellogg-Briand's no-enforcement clause, US investment dependency) to support both; explains why historians disagree (perspective, era of writing, which events they weight most). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Notes some differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was the Dawes Plan the most important reason for European stability in the 1920s? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Dawes Plan (ending Ruhr crisis, enabling reparations to function) against other factors (Locarno diplomacy, League admission of Germany, Kellogg-Briand idealism); acknowledges the fragility of US-investment-dependent stability; uses named historians or schools where appropriate. Secure: Clear argument addressing the Dawes Plan and at least two other factors with specific evidence. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence, possibly focused too narrowly on one agreement. Emerging: Descriptive account of the agreements. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Enabling Act (1933).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate supporting detail (e.g. gave Hitler the power to make laws without Reichstag approval for four years, passed on 23 March 1933 with a 444 to 94 majority). Secure: Names a valid feature with some supporting detail. Developing: States a point without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. SS and Gestapo units killed at least 85 people, among them the SA leader Ernst Röhm, who was shot on 1 July). Secure: Names a valid feature with some detail. Developing: States a feature without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Enabling Act was crucial to Hitler's consolidation of power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses why the Enabling Act was decisive — gave Hitler legal power to bypass the Reichstag, enabled Gleichschaltung, destroyed party opposition, banned trade unions — and places it within the broader sequence (Fire Decree → election → Enabling Act → dictatorship). Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Hitler was able to consolidate his power in the years 1933–1934.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed steps, each with precise evidence and analysis of how it contributed to consolidation (e.g. Enabling Act removing parliamentary constraints; Night of the Long Knives securing army support). Secure: Two steps with relevant evidence. Developing: Two steps with limited analysis. Emerging: One step or vague points.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of the army in enabling Hitler to establish his dictatorship in 1933–1934?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs the army's role (acceptance of Night of the Long Knives, oath of 2 August 1934) against other factors (Enabling Act, Reichstag Fire Decree, Gleichschaltung, Catholic Centre Party vote, Communist/SPD suppression). Substantiated judgement on the balance. Secure: Identifies army's role and compares to other factors with evidence. Developing: Describes army's role without comparative analysis. Emerging: Descriptive, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that Hitler's consolidation of power in 1933–1934 was primarily the result of terror and intimidation rather than popular support. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument covering role of terror (SA intimidation in March 1933 elections, arrest of KPD/SPD leaders, Night of the Long Knives) alongside factors that suggest genuine or manufactured consent (43.9% NSDAP vote in March 1933, Catholic Centre Party vote for Enabling Act, army oath, trade union suppression accepted by many workers). Precise evidence throughout; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed with relevant evidence. Developing: Unbalanced or insufficiently evidenced. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Act of Supremacy 1534 mattered for the English Church.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. it made the king the only Supreme Head of the Church of England, so no English case could go to Rome; it handed the Crown the power to appoint bishops and change Church law. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Reformation Parliament was so important between 1529 and 1536.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. the Submission of the Clergy (1532) stopped the Church making its own law without the king; the Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) cut off appeals to Rome, so Cranmer could rule on the marriage in an English court. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Henry VIII sought an annulment from Catherine of Aragon.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with evidence, linked (e.g. need for male heir + Pope's political constraints = Henry's determination to use Parliament). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason developed. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why some people refused to accept the royal supremacy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons (theological conviction + personal loyalty to the universal Church) with evidence; links outcomes (execution under Treason Act). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'The Act in Restraint of Appeals 1533 was the turning point in ending papal authority in England.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. In the exam this question comes with sources; here, answer from your own knowledge. Mastering: weighs the 1533 Act (England declared an empire, appeals to Rome ended, the annulment made possible) against the Submission of the Clergy, the Act of Supremacy and the Treason Act; clear judgement. Secure: two Acts compared with evidence. Developing: one Act developed. Emerging: narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Thomas Cromwell was the man most responsible for the break with Rome.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Mastering: weighs Cromwell's drafting and management of the statutes against Henry's own determination, the Pope's refusal and Cranmer's ruling; supported judgement. Secure: two factors with evidence. Developing: one factor developed. Emerging: description.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the New Model Army was more effective than Parliament's earlier armies.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. it was a national force under one commander, Sir Thomas Fairfax, and it was paid regularly, unlike the regional armies it replaced. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Naseby in June 1645 was a disaster for Charles I.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons, e.g. Cromwell's cavalry held its discipline and turned on the Royalist foot, so about 5,000 were captured; Charles's private letters were also taken, revealing talks with Irish Catholics and foreign powers. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament created the New Model Army in 1645.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple causes (Manchester and Essex's failures, Cromwell's criticism of Manchester, need for unified command, Self-Denying Ordinance removing MP commanders) linked together with clear analysis of which was most important. Secure: Two causes with evidence. Developing: One cause or two briefly stated. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: The Self-Denying Ordinance was the most important reason Parliament won the First Civil War. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the Self-Denying Ordinance (cleared ineffective commanders) against other factors: Solemn League and Covenant (Scottish intervention), New Model Army (professional unified force), Naseby (decisive victory), Royalist weaknesses (logistics, correspondence capture). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides examined with evidence. Developing: One side primarily. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Marston Moor (1644) was significant for Parliament.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (north secured permanently, Royalist north destroyed, Cromwell's reputation established, Scottish alliance proved valuable, morale shift). Linked argument. Secure: Two reasons with detail. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament and its Scottish allies signed the Solemn League and Covenant in 1643.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Scottish motivation (defend Presbyterianism, obtain English commitment to reform), Parliament's motivation (need for army to stop Royalist advances), and how both sides had different expectations of the agreement. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple answer.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Magna Carta (1215).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific clause or principle (e.g. Clause 39 established that no free man could be imprisoned without lawful judgement) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. this was a direct response to John's arbitrary use of royal courts to punish barons who opposed him). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to 'limiting the king' without specifics. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the parliament called by Simon de Montfort in 1265.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. it included knights from each county — the first parliament to represent ordinary landowners below the baronial class; it included burgesses from towns — bringing in representatives of the trading community for the first time). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the barons rebelled against King John and forced him to seal Magna Carta in 1215.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more well-developed reasons with specific evidence (loss of Normandy 1204 damaged baronial French estates and reflected military failure John blamed on barons; John raised taxation beyond feudal custom to fund his wars, demanding payments the barons saw as illegal; John manipulated royal courts and took noble hostages, violating accepted norms of justice — Clause 39 directly addressed this). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped ones. Emerging: narrative of John being unpopular without analytical reasons.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the development of Parliament in the thirteenth century was significant for the future of royal power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains how each step was significant for later constitutional development (Magna Carta established the principle of legal limits on kingship — reissued multiple times, it became a constitutional reference point; de Montfort's 1265 parliament established that governance could include non-noble representatives; Edward I's Model Parliament 1295 made representative taxation consent a regular practice — setting a precedent monarchs later struggled to reverse). Secure: two steps explained with specific evidence. Developing: describes parliamentary development accurately but does not explain why each step mattered. Emerging: vague points about Parliament becoming more powerful.

practice_questions.text: How far did Magna Carta and the growth of Parliament change the relationship between the monarchy and its subjects in the period 1199-1399? [You may consider: Magna Carta 1215; the parliaments of 1265 and 1295; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument weighing change against continuity — change: Magna Carta limited arbitrary royal power in principle; de Montfort's 1265 parliament included commoners; Model Parliament established taxation by consent; Richard II's deposition 1399 showed parliament could be used to remove a monarch. Continuity: kings still dominated; John rejected Magna Carta immediately; de Montfort was crushed; Parliament met at royal summons only; Wars of the Roses showed military power still trumped constitutional principles. Overall judgement required. Secure: both sides argued with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes the growth of Parliament without weighing change vs continuity. Emerging: narrative account without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the key events in the emergence of Parliament between 1215 and 1295.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points in sequence (Magna Carta 1215 — barons force limits on John; Provisions of Oxford 1258 — baronial council imposed on Henry III; de Montfort's parliament 1265 — first with knights and burgesses; Model Parliament 1295 — Edward I formalises representative assembly for taxation). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Parliament developing.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Nelson Mandela's statement from the dock at the Rivonia Trial.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the statement AND gives a precise feature, e.g. Mandela acknowledged ANC sabotage but argued it was a last resort after peaceful methods failed; or he concluded by saying he was prepared to die for a democratic South Africa. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to a speech. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of conditions on Robben Island for political prisoners.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names Robben Island AND gives a precise feature, e.g. prisoners did hard labour in a limestone quarry, or they were allowed one letter and one visit every six months. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to harsh prison conditions. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Rivonia Trial had consequences for both sides of the apartheid conflict.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed points explaining benefits to the government (ANC leadership imprisoned, movement silenced internally) AND costs (international martyrdom, Mandela's dock statement, UN resolutions). Each point developed with specific evidence. Secure: Both sides covered with supporting detail. Developing: One side only developed, or two underdeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of the trial with limited analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Rivonia Trial is considered a significant turning point in the history of apartheid.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons with precise evidence — e.g. (1) imprisonment of the ANC's top leadership created a 'long silence' inside South Africa; (2) Mandela's dock statement became a global text boosting the ANC internationally. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or descriptive answer.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Rivonia Trial weakened resistance inside South Africa for more than a decade.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with precise evidence, e.g. the trial removed the ANC's most experienced leaders for a generation; the underground network left behind was too small and too closely watched to organise mass action. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of the trial.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Rivonia Trial succeed in destroying the anti-apartheid movement? Use your knowledge of the period 1964–1976 in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing the degree of damage (leadership imprisoned, 'long silence', MK decimated) against evidence of continued resistance (BCM emerging in late 1960s, exile organisation under Tambo, Soweto 1976 showing new generation); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of the trial and its aftermath with limited weighing. Emerging: Narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Jim Crow laws in the American South.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names a specific Jim Crow provision with accurate detail, e.g. literacy tests required voters to read and interpret complex legal passages, applied selectively to prevent Black Americans from registering to vote. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to segregation. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the legal and political obstacles facing African Americans in the late 1940s and early 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) poll taxes excluded most Black voters who could not afford the fee; (2) the Plessy v Ferguson doctrine (1896) gave constitutional cover to segregation by declaring 'separate but equal' facilities legal. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the NAACP chose to challenge school segregation through the courts rather than through other methods.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — legal strategy built on the precedents of Sweatt v Painter and Shelley v Kraemer; mass protest was dangerous in the South; courts offered a mechanism to overturn state laws that Congress would not; Marshall's expertise lay in constitutional law. Shows how reasons interconnect. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes the strategy without explaining the choice of method. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why voting rights were so important to African Americans in the South in the late 1940s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) without the vote, African Americans had no way to elect politicians who would change discriminatory laws at state level, leaving them permanently subject to Jim Crow; (2) voting was a symbol of full citizenship — its denial reinforced second-class status and the accompanying discrimination in education, employment and housing. Each reason includes specific evidence and explanation. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: Two reasons identified without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was Brown v Board of Education in improving the position of African Americans?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis — significant because it overturned Plessy and provided a legal basis for desegregation; gave the civil rights movement moral authority; showed the Supreme Court could be an agent of change. But limitations: implementation was resisted (Brown II 1955 allowed 'all deliberate speed'; Little Rock 1957 showed federal force was still needed); the ruling addressed schools, not voting rights or employment; mass protest and further legislation were still required. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Brown without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the challenges facing African Americans in the USA in the years before Brown v Board of Education 1954.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering legal segregation (Jim Crow, Plessy), disfranchisement (poll tax, literacy tests, white primaries), economic disadvantage (employment, housing, redlining) and violence (lynching, sundown towns). Reaches an integrated judgement about which challenges were most significant or interconnected. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several challenges with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes conditions with limited structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the African presence in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Africans lived as free individuals in Tudor England (1); for example, John Blanke was a royal trumpeter who received wages and petitioned for a pay rise from Henry VIII (1). Feature 2: Africans worked in a range of skilled occupations (1); Reasonable Blackman was an independent silk-weaver in Southwark, documented in London parish records (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why South Asian people began arriving in England from the seventeenth century onwards.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons fully developed with specific evidence. Reason 1: The East India Company (chartered 1600) recruited Lascar seamen from Bengal and other coastal regions; as ships rotated through English ports, some sailors remained and formed communities in port districts. Reason 2: East India Company officials returning to England brought South Asian servants — ayahs (nursemaids) and other domestic workers — who were sometimes abandoned on arrival and formed vulnerable migrant communities. Secure: Both reasons explained with evidence. Developing: One reason explained well. Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which alien residents in medieval England contributed to the economy.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: Flemish weavers brought advanced textile techniques to East Anglia and Kent (1), driving growth in the English cloth industry (1); Hanseatic League merchants operated from the Steelyard in London (1), integrating England into European trading networks (1); Italian merchants from Florence and Genoa dominated luxury goods trade through Lombard Street (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the experiences of African individuals in Tudor England varied so widely.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies that diversity of experience reflected diversity of legal status and occupation — John Blanke was a salaried professional with standing; Reasonable Blackman an independent craftsman; later enslaved Africans brought by colonists had no legal protections. Connects this to the development of Atlantic slavery as a distinct system from the earlier presence of free African individuals. Secure: Explains variation with at least two specific contrasting examples. Developing: Notes some variation with limited evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account without explanation.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that African migrants in early modern England were primarily victims of racial discrimination? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that balances evidence of agency (John Blanke, Reasonable Blackman, John Lok's interpreters) against evidence of discrimination (Elizabeth I's proclamations, later development of slavery, vulnerability of Lascars and ayahs); engages with Miranda Kaufmann and Onyeka Nubia's historical research; avoids both uncritical celebration and flattening all experiences as victimhood. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides. Developing: Some awareness of complexity with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the chartering of the East India Company in 1600 led to new patterns of migration to England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two patterns explained with specific causal links — Lascar seamen recruited in India arrived in English ports and sometimes settled when stranded; South Asian domestic workers brought back by Company officials formed vulnerable communities. Explains how the Company's commercial operations directly caused these movements. Secure: Two patterns explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One pattern explained. Emerging: General statements about trade and migration.

practice_questions.text: Describe two causes of Prohibition in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct cause, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: the temperance movement’s long campaign against alcohol on moral and religious grounds; nativist hostility to immigrant drinking cultures; Progressive arguments that alcohol caused urban poverty, domestic abuse and crime.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Prohibition failed to eliminate alcohol consumption in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the Prohibition Bureau was underfunded with roughly 1,500 agents for the entire country, making enforcement impossible, and agents were susceptible to bribery from criminal networks like Capone’s; speakeasies multiplied to an estimated 20,000–30,000 in New York alone, supplied by bootleggers smuggling from Canada and the Caribbean). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both reasons identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why organised crime grew so rapidly during the Prohibition era.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies and explains how Prohibition created a market for illegal alcohol that criminal networks could exploit; the enormous profits generated (Capone’s estimated $60 million annual income) funded expansion into other criminal activities; corruption of police and officials removed legal obstacles; violence enforced territory. Secure: Two or more factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One factor explained, others named. Emerging: General statement about crime increasing without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the St Valentine's Day Massacre of 1929.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: it took place in Chicago in February 1929; seven members of the Bugs Moran gang were shot dead; the gunmen were believed to be linked to Al Capone; it showed the violent competition to control bootlegging.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that Prohibition was a complete failure? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges partial successes (reduced alcohol consumption in early years, lower cirrhosis rates, fewer arrests for public drunkenness) before explaining why overall failure is the stronger conclusion (widespread non-compliance, growth of organised crime, corruption of officials, eventual repeal in 1933); uses specific evidence throughout and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument addressing both success and failure with relevant evidence. Developing: Some awareness of both sides with basic evidence; may be one-sided. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are given in this section.

practice_questions.text: Sources A and B give different views of Prohibition. Source A says it was a misguided moral experiment that gave power to criminals. Source B says it achieved real health and social benefits that were undermined by poor enforcement. How far do the two sources agree? Use both sources and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (moral vs. pragmatic framing, role of enforcement, health data); tests both against own knowledge (crime statistics for A; cirrhosis and domestic violence data for B); explains why the two views differ (different evidence base, writing from different periods, urban vs. rural perspective). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955–1956.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Identifies a specific feature with detail, e.g. the boycott lasted 381 days and African Americans, who made up about 75% of bus passengers, stayed off the buses, causing serious economic damage to the bus company. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to the boycott. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the roles played by civil rights organisations in the movement between 1954 and 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) the NAACP used court cases like Brown v Board to overturn segregation laws; (2) the SCLC, founded by King in 1957, used the Black church network to coordinate non-violent direct action campaigns. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Martin Luther King Jr emerged as the leading figure of the civil rights movement between 1955 and 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — his oratorical skill demonstrated at the MIA meetings; his philosophy of non-violent direct action gave the movement a coherent and effective strategy; the Montgomery boycott provided a high-profile success to build on; SCLC gave him an organisational base. Shows how these factors combined. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes King without explaining why he rose to leadership. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Little Rock crisis of 1957 was a significant moment in the civil rights movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) it demonstrated that the federal government would use military force to uphold Brown, setting a precedent for future federal intervention; (2) images of soldiers escorting nine children past jeering crowds were seen globally, exposing Southern resistance to an international audience during the Cold War. Each reason includes specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence and explanation. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of Rosa Parks in the development of the civil rights movement?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis — significant because her arrest sparked the 381-day boycott that proved Black economic power and launched King; her status as an NAACP activist made her a carefully chosen catalyst. But places her significance in context: Brown had created the legal framework; the NAACP had planned the campaign; she was one part of a coordinated strategy. Compares her significance to King, the NAACP, and the movement as a whole. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Parks without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the developments in the civil rights movement between 1954 and 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering Brown's ruling and resistance (Little Rock 1957), the Montgomery boycott (Parks, King, Browder v Gayle), the role of organisations (NAACP, SCLC, SNCC), Greensboro sit-ins, and Emmett Till's galvanising effect. Reaches an integrated judgement about what was achieved and what remained undone by 1960. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several developments with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events in chronological order with limited analysis. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Jim Crow system of laws in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: legal segregation in schools, transport and public spaces; the 1896 Plessy v Ferguson ruling that ‘separate but equal’ was constitutional; denial of the vote through literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Ku Klux Klan grew so rapidly in the early 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. post-war anxiety and the Red Summer of 1919 created a climate of racial and social fear in which the Klan’s message of ‘100 per cent Americanism’ appealed to white Protestants threatened by immigration and African American assertion; the Klan’s broadened appeal — targeting Catholics, Jews, and immigrants as well as Black Americans — allowed it to recruit millions outside the South, reaching 4–6 million by 1924–25). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Tulsa Race Massacre of 1921 is significant for understanding racial violence in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the significance of the Tulsa Massacre in showing the scale of organised racial violence (at least 39 dead, 35 blocks destroyed); the active role of deputised civilians and the failure of authorities to protect Black residents; the deliberate suppression of the event from public memory for decades; and what this reveals about the systematic nature of racial violence rather than isolated incidents. Secure: Two or more dimensions explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One dimension explained, others listed. Emerging: General statement about the massacre’s seriousness without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: it promoted Black economic self-sufficiency and Black-owned businesses; it ran a steamship company; it promoted a ‘Back to Africa’ movement calling for a new nation in Africa.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the 1920s was a decade of racial backlash in the United States? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges evidence of backlash (Klan revival, Tulsa Massacre, Red Summer, Jim Crow, failed anti-lynching legislation) while also recognising African American resistance and cultural achievement (NAACP campaigns, Garvey movement, Harlem Renaissance, Great Migration); uses specific evidence throughout and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument addressing both backlash and resistance with relevant evidence. Developing: Some awareness of both with basic evidence; may be one-sided. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are given in this section.

practice_questions.text: Sources A and B give different views of the Ku Klux Klan revival. Source A says the Klan reflected deep-rooted racism in American society and government. Source B says it was primarily a product of specific post-war anxieties that disappeared once conditions changed. How far do the two sources agree? Use both sources and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (structural racism vs. contingent anxiety, permanence vs. transience of the threat); tests both against own knowledge (persistence of Jim Crow and failure of anti-lynching bills for A; Klan collapse after Stephenson scandal and specific post-war context for B); explains why the two views differ (different focus on cause, different evidence base, period of writing). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the people's communes established during the Great Leap Forward.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. size, abolition of private plots, communal eating). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without clear detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the First Five-Year Plan (1953–57).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise detail (e.g. Soviet model, heavy industry focus, Soviet technical assistance, output gains). Secure: Two features, each with some supporting detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Great Leap Forward caused such a catastrophic famine.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons linked together (e.g. agricultural labour diverted to steel, false reporting after Peng Dehuai's purge, commune system abolishing private incentives). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the purge of Peng Dehuai for the continuation of the Great Leap Forward.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of significance (immediate chilling effect on honest reporting, longer-term famine continuation, signals to future critics); counter-argument addressed. Secure: Clear argument about significance with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis. Emerging: Describes the purge with minimal argument about significance.

practice_questions.text: How far was the Great Leap Forward the main cause of the 1959–62 famine? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing multiple causes (policy failure, reporting system, purge of critics, weather as minor factor); specific evidence; considers whether other causes were more or less important. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from multiple causes; some weighing of relative importance. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Dazhai commune was significant as a case study in the failure of the Great Leap Forward.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons explaining both what Dazhai represented symbolically and what its later exposure revealed about systematic falsification. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how indentured servitude differed from chattel slavery.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. indenture was a contract for a fixed term of roughly four to seven years, after which the servant was free; enslaved Africans were property for life and their children were enslaved too). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why some people from the British Isles chose to emigrate to the Americas in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. William Penn's Pennsylvania offered religious tolerance to dissenters; Ulster Scots left because of rack-renting landlords and discrimination against Presbyterians). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why different groups emigrated from the British Isles for different reasons in the period 1688–c.1730.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation covering at least two distinct groups (e.g. Ulster Scots, Irish Catholics, transported convicts) with precise evidence linking push and pull factors. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one group's reasons explained in depth. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: 'Forced emigration shaped Britain's American colonies more than voluntary emigration in this period.' How far do you agree? Use Sources A and B [supplied in the exam] and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs both sides, uses precise evidence (transportation after the Bloody Assizes and under the 1718 act, the Wild Geese, Penn's Pennsylvania and the Ulster Scots), works both sources into the argument, and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence and some use of the sources. Developing: Some argument; sources described rather than used. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence. Five of the 25 marks are for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why indentured servitude declined on large plantations from the 1680s onwards.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing planters found enslaved Africans more profitable (lifelong, heritable labour) than indentured servants (time-limited contracts with subsequent freedom and land claims), with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Ulster Scots emigrated to North America from the 1680s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. rack-renting landlords and the Woollen Act of 1699, which damaged Irish textile exports; religious discrimination against Presbyterians). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the Wall Street Crash of 1929 affected Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each effect scores 1 mark for identification and 1 for specific detail. Examples: US banks recalled loans to Germany (1), causing the Dawes Plan circular payment system to collapse (1); German unemployment rose from approximately 1.3 million (1929) to roughly 6 million by 1932 (1); the Nazi Party's vote share rose from 2.6% (1928) to 37.4% (July 1932) (1) as desperate voters sought radical alternatives (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 damaged international relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed with causal analysis — it triggered retaliatory tariff increases from other countries (trade wars contracting global commerce); it damaged economic interdependence that had underpinned 1920s stability, making international co-operation harder when crises arose. Secure: Both explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained, one identified. Emerging: General statement about economic nationalism without specific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the political crisis in Germany between 1930 and 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and up to 2 marks for specific supporting detail. Feature 1: The Nazi Party's electoral support surged (1); from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932 as economic hardship grew (1). Feature 2: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution was used increasingly to govern by emergency decree (1); bypassing the Reichstag and weakening parliamentary democracy (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Great Depression made it harder for the League of Nations to maintain international order.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Multiple interlocking causes — economic nationalism (Smoot-Hawley) reduced co-operation; the Manchurian crisis showed the League could not act decisively; the rise of authoritarian governments hostile to collective security weakened the League's membership; Britain and France were too focused on domestic recovery to take strong action abroad. Connects causes to show systemic undermining of collective security. Secure: Two or more causes with explanation. Developing: One cause explained, others listed. Emerging: General reference to the Depression without causal link to the League.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of why authoritarian governments rose in Europe after 1929. Interpretation A argues the Depression was the decisive cause, removing economic stability and driving desperate populations towards extremist movements. Interpretation B contends that pre-existing political weaknesses — such as Versailles grievances and short democratic traditions — were equally important. How far do the interpretations differ and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies that Interpretation A emphasises economic causation while B focuses on structural/historical factors; uses own knowledge (Weimar's hyperinflation legacy, Versailles resentment, Smoot-Hawley consequences) to support both; explains why historians disagree (which factors they weight most). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Notes some differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was the Wall Street Crash the main cause of the breakdown of international order between 1929 and 1933? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Wall Street Crash (Dawes Plan collapse, German unemployment, extremist politics) against other factors (pre-existing Versailles grievances, Smoot-Hawley tariff choices, Japanese militarism, League structural weakness); draws on named interpretations or schools where possible; reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: Clear argument with multiple causes and specific evidence. Developing: Some argument, possibly over-focused on the Crash. Emerging: Descriptive account. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Valor Ecclesiasticus was useful to the Crown in 1535.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. it recorded the income of every Church institution, so the Crown knew exactly what it stood to gain; it showed which houses fell under £200 a year, which set the target for the first closures. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Comperta was useful to Cromwell in 1536.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. its charges of immorality gave Parliament a moral case for closing houses; it was ready just as the first Suppression Bill was put before members, so the accusations arrived when they were needed. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell ordered both the Valor Ecclesiasticus and the Visitation of the Monasteries in 1535.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons linked (financial benefit from seizure + moral cover for Parliament); notes the political purpose behind each document. Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason developed. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why historians disagree about the reliability of the Comperta.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues both sides — political motivation undermines reliability vs. some genuine pre-existing problems evidenced by bishops' registers; well-supported judgement. Secure: Two reasons for/against reliability. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'The Valor Ecclesiasticus mattered more than the Comperta in bringing about the dissolution.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. In the exam this question comes with sources; here, answer from your own knowledge. Mastering: weighs the financial case (income mapped house by house, the £200 threshold) against the moral case (charges of misconduct, rushed visits), and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: both documents argued with evidence. Developing: one document developed. Emerging: description.

practice_questions.text: 'Thomas Cromwell made the dissolution of the monasteries possible.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Mastering: weighs Cromwell's surveys, visitors and management of Parliament against Henry's need for money, the earlier break with Rome and the appetite of the gentry for land; supported judgement. Secure: two factors with evidence. Developing: one factor developed. Emerging: description.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Gestapo.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the Gestapo was the Secret State Police, created in Prussia in 1933 and placed under SS control in 1934, with powers to arrest and detain without trial under 'protective custody'). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the SS under Himmler's leadership.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. Himmler became Chief of German Police in 1936, which put the SS in charge of every police force in Germany). Secure: Names a valid feature with some detail. Developing: States a feature without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Gestapo was so effective at controlling the German population.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the role of civilian denunciations alongside the Gestapo's extraordinary powers (protective custody, no judicial oversight) and the culture of fear it created. Draws on Gellately/Johnson scholarship to complicate the assumption of omniscient surveillance. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Nazi terror state was able to control the German population in the years 1933–1939.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed methods with precise evidence (e.g. Gestapo/denunciation system; concentration camp threat for political opponents; People's Court destroying judicial independence; SD monitoring of public opinion). Analysis shows how each method worked. Secure: Two methods with relevant evidence. Developing: Two methods listed without analysis. Emerging: One method or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of civilian denunciations in making the Nazi terror state effective?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs denunciations (Gellately/Johnson findings on Gestapo's small size and reliance on public reports) against other factors (SS institutional power, concentration camp threat, People's Court, SD intelligence). Substantiated judgement on relative significance. Secure: Considers denunciations and other factors with evidence. Developing: Describes denunciations without comparison. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that the Nazi terror state functioned primarily through fear of the regime rather than through active co-operation from ordinary Germans. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence of top-down terror (SS, Gestapo powers, concentration camps, show trials) against evidence of participatory co-operation (denunciations driving most Gestapo investigations, SD relying on public informants, public attendance at racial persecution). Uses historiographical insight (Gellately, Johnson) to support argument. Precise evidence; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Huguenot contribution to English society after 1685.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Huguenot weavers established a sophisticated silk-weaving trade in Spitalfields, east London (1); families like the Courtaulds grew into major industrial firms (1). Feature 2: Huguenot silversmiths brought high-quality French metalworking techniques to London (1); Paul de Lamerie became one of England's most celebrated silversmiths (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Oliver Cromwell permitted the readmission of Jews in 1656.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons fully developed. Reason 1: Commercial motivation — Cromwell saw that Dutch and Sephardic Jewish merchants had driven Amsterdam's trading success and wanted similar economic benefits for England; Jewish merchant networks could improve English overseas trade. Reason 2: Religious motivation — Puritan millenarian theology held that the conversion of the Jews was a precondition for Christ's return; readmission was seen as a step towards that goal. Secure: Both reasons explained with evidence. Developing: One reason well explained. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Huguenot refugees were received more positively than the Palatines who arrived in 1709.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear multi-causal explanation — Huguenots arrived gradually and brought skilled trades (silk, silversmithing); shared Protestantism generated sympathy; anti-French sentiment after 1685 made them politically useful. Palatines arrived in one large wave (13,000 in summer 1709), many were poor labourers, they strained charitable resources, and public debate about cost quickly turned opinion. Secure: Explains at least two contrasting factors. Developing: Notes the different reception without fully explaining the causes. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two pieces of evidence that show the Huguenots successfully integrated into English society.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: Huguenot surnames like Courtauld and Du Cane became established English family names within two or three generations (1); the Courtauld family became major textile industrialists, fully integrated into English economic life (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the reception of refugees in seventeenth and eighteenth-century England was primarily determined by religious sympathy? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument testing the claim against economic evidence — Jewish readmission was de facto and quiet, driven more by commerce than theology; Huguenots were welcomed for their skills as well as their Protestantism; Palatines were fellow Protestants but faced ambivalent reception because of their numbers and economic needs. Concludes that religion was one factor among several including economics, numbers and perceived cultural similarity. Secure: Clear argument with evidence across at least two communities. Developing: Some comparison with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Huguenot settlement of the 1680s and 1690s changed English industry and culture.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two changes explained with specific causal links. Change 1: Spitalfields silk industry created — Huguenot weavers introduced advanced techniques previously absent from England at scale; their skills drove significant economic growth in east London. Change 2: Silversmithing and design transformed — craftspeople like Paul de Lamerie brought French Baroque and Rococo styles that influenced English decorative arts. Secure: Two changes explained with evidence. Developing: One change explained. Emerging: General statements.

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages Elizabeth I gained by using privateers instead of open war with Spain.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. using privateers allowed Elizabeth to harass Spanish shipping and gain wealth while maintaining diplomatic flexibility and deniability). Developing: vague (e.g. 'it was safer').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Spanish Armada's failure in 1588.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. English fireships scattered the fleet from its anchorage off Calais; storms wrecked many ships on the long route home around Scotland and Ireland. Developing: identifies features without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why privateering was controversial in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers mixed economic impact (profit for investors, disruption to legitimate trade), security risks (Spanish reprisals, Cornish raid 1595), moral questions (Hawkins and the slave trade), diplomatic problems (risking all-out war). Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the wars with Spain increased Parliament's power during Elizabeth's reign.
