practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links war costs to need for Parliamentary taxation, Elizabeth's resistance but ultimate concessions (monopolies 1601), and the precedent this set for Stuart relations with Parliament. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the wars with Spain strengthen Elizabeth I's power and prestige? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — balances strengthening (Armada propaganda, national identity, Drake's prestige, treasure) against weakening (debt, Parliamentary pressure, monopolies crisis, costly Irish wars), reaching a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument covering both sides. Developing: Mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Francis Drake's circumnavigation (1577–80) was significant for England's conflict with Spain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains commercial significance (treasure, investor profits), symbolic significance (challenge to Spanish maritime dominance), political significance (Elizabeth's knighthood demonstrated Crown backing), and military significance (disrupted Spanish silver supply). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Leveller programme was radical for the 1640s.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. the Agreement of the People asked for a wider male franchise, and the Levellers argued that every man subject to the law should help choose the government, not only property owners. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Putney Debates of 1647 ended without agreement.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons, e.g. the agitators presented the Agreement of the People and asked for a wider franchise, while Ireton insisted that only men with a permanent fixed interest should vote, so neither side would move. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Levellers gained support within the New Model Army in 1647.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more reasons explained with evidence (religious culture of the army, pay grievances, Lilburne's pamphlets, political vacuum after First Civil War, rank and file felt excluded from post-war settlement). Linked argument. Secure: Two causes. Developing: One cause. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: The Levellers were the most significant radical group of the 1640s. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument comparing Levellers (scale, programme, army influence, Putney Debates) with Diggers (more radical challenge to property) and Quakers (religious radicalism, longer survival). Reaches a supported judgement about relative significance. Secure: Compares two or more groups with evidence. Developing: Mainly discusses Levellers with limited comparison. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why radical religious and political groups emerged in England in the late 1640s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (breakdown of censorship, army as vehicle for radical ideas, religious pluralism encouraged by civil war, social dislocation, Calvinist emphasis on individual faith). Linked and developed. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament and the army suppressed the Levellers after the Putney Debates.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains why Leveller demands threatened property, social order and army discipline; Ireton's ideological opposition; Cromwell's priority for stability; Leveller mutinies gave military justification. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Black Consciousness Movement in South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names BCM AND gives a precise feature, e.g. it argued that psychological liberation — rejecting internalised inferiority — must precede political liberation; or SASO was founded in 1969 by Steve Biko to organise black students independently. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to black pride or student movement. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Durban strike wave of 1973.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the Durban strikes AND gives a precise feature, e.g. about 100,000 workers walked out between January and March 1973, or the strikes were largely spontaneous with no single organising body. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to workers striking. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Black Consciousness Movement emerged in South Africa in the late 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the Rivonia imprisonments had created an organisational vacuum inside South Africa; (2) the ANC and PAC were banned, leaving a political space for a new approach; (3) Bantu Education had concentrated politically active students in black universities. Each with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two underdeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the growth of trade unions in the early 1970s challenged the apartheid system.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed points — e.g. (1) the Durban strikes demonstrated that black workers could organise collectively even though black trade unions had no legal recognition; (2) they forced employers and government to recognise that the pass system and low wages were economically unsustainable. Secure: Two points with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-explained point. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Steve Biko's death in police custody in September 1977 damaged the apartheid government.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with precise evidence, e.g. the government's hunger-strike story was shown to be false, so its word could not be trusted; the killing of a well-known young leader turned foreign opinion further against apartheid and helped bring the UN arms embargo. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of Biko's death.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Black Consciousness Movement in keeping resistance to apartheid alive during the 1970s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing BCM's significance (filled organisational vacuum, shaped Soweto generation, international impact of Biko's death) against other factors (ANC in exile under Tambo, Durban strike-driven trade unionism, continuing ANC underground); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of BCM with limited comparison to other factors. Emerging: Narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Act of Supremacy (1534).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. it made Henry VIII the Supreme Head of the Church of England) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. it ended papal authority in England, making it treasonous to deny Henry's religious supremacy). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to Henry becoming head of the Church. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Elizabethan Religious Settlement (1559).
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. the Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth Supreme Governor — a softer title than Henry VIII's 'Supreme Head', designed to be more acceptable to Catholics; the Act of Uniformity imposed the Book of Common Prayer, giving the Protestant settlement statutory force). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Henry VIII used Parliament to achieve the English Reformation rather than acting through royal decree alone.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (statute law was harder to reverse than royal decree — giving the Reformation permanence; Parliamentary approval gave the break with Rome legal force that could be used to punish opposition through treason charges; Cromwell's management of Parliament made it an effective legislative tool; routing the Reformation through Parliament also confirmed Parliament's role in major constitutional changes — a double-edged consequence). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped reasons. Emerging: describes the Reformation without addressing why Parliament was used.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Elizabeth I's management of Parliament faced growing challenges by the 1590s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains two or more factors with specific evidence (the 'Puritan choir' of MPs persistently introduced Church reform bills Elizabeth regarded as infringing on royal prerogative, which she had to veto repeatedly; the monopolies dispute of 1601 led to Elizabeth's Golden Speech conceding that her advisers had misinformed her — a rare public admission; the succession question never resolved, creating anxiety among MPs that a Catholic heir could undo the Protestant settlement). Secure: two factors with relevant evidence. Developing: describes parliamentary tensions without explaining their causes or significance. Emerging: vague reference to Parliament becoming more powerful.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Reformation increase the power of Parliament in Tudor England? [You may consider: the Reformation Parliament; Elizabeth I's management of Parliament; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument with evidence from across the Tudor period — change: Reformation Parliament legislated on the most fundamental questions of Church and state; dissolution of monasteries created a gentry class with stake in Protestant Parliament; Parliament's legislative role grew in sophistication under Cromwell's management; Elizabeth had to use prerogative carefully and concede on monopolies. Continuity: monarchs still controlled when Parliament met; Elizabeth successfully blocked Church reform bills; Parliament met only when summoned. Overall judgement required. Secure: argues both sides with specific evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes Parliamentary role accurately but does not weigh increase in power against continuities. Emerging: narrative of Tudor history without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main ways Henry VIII used Parliament to carry out the English Reformation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points (Reformation Parliament 1529-36 passed a series of Acts cutting ties with Rome; Act of Supremacy 1534 made Henry Supreme Head of the Church; Cromwell managed the parliamentary programme; dissolution of the monasteries 1536-40 carried out by statute; Treasons Act 1534 made denial of supremacy capital). Secure: two or three relevant points with some detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Henry using Parliament.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Freedom Rides of 1961.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the Freedom Rides and gives specific detail, e.g. interracial teams rode interstate buses into the South to challenge segregated terminals; in Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of the buses. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to protesters on buses. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Civil Rights Act 1964.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) the Act banned racial discrimination in public accommodations including hotels, restaurants and cinemas; (2) Title VII banned employment discrimination and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce it. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Birmingham campaign of 1963 was so important in pushing the federal government to act on civil rights.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple causes with specific evidence — Bull Connor's use of fire hoses and dogs on non-violent protesters (including children) was filmed and broadcast; Kennedy called the scenes 'shameful' and announced legislation; the strategy of provoking a violent response to expose Southern brutality had worked. Shows the deliberate calculation behind the campaign. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes events without explaining impact. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why President Johnson was more effective than Kennedy in passing civil rights legislation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) Johnson had decades of congressional experience and knew how to manage Senate procedure, something Kennedy lacked; (2) Kennedy's assassination created a political moment in which Johnson could invoke the dead president's legacy to overcome Southern filibuster. Each reason includes specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the March on Washington in the development of the civil rights movement?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis — significant because it was the largest political demonstration in US history to that point (250,000 people), it showed the movement's breadth and coalition character, and it kept civil rights at the top of the political agenda. But places it in context: Kennedy had already announced legislation after Birmingham; King's speech was powerful symbolically but the real legislative change required Johnson's skill; the Act would not pass until a year later. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes the march without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the roles of government and protest in securing the Civil Rights Act 1964 and the Voting Rights Act 1965.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay weighing protest (Freedom Rides, Birmingham, Selma, March on Washington) against governmental action (Kennedy's reluctance and then announcement; Johnson's legislative skill; Supreme Court rulings). Reaches an integrated judgement about which was more important or how they interacted. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several factors with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited analytical structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the Abyssinian crisis of 1935-1936 damaged the League of Nations.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each way scores 1 mark for identification and 1 for specific detail. Examples: sanctions excluded key resources such as oil and coal (1), meaning they failed to halt Italy's military campaign (1); the secret Hoare-Laval Pact (1) proposed rewarding Italy with most of Abyssinia and caused a major political scandal when it leaked (1); Italy completed the conquest of Abyssinia and the League lifted sanctions (1), demonstrating it could not enforce collective security against a major power (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Britain and France did not prevent Germany from remilitarising the Rhineland in March 1936.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed — French military argued full mobilisation was required and the government was unwilling to order it; British leaders believed Germany had legitimate grievances about Versailles and were not willing to go to war over German troops entering German territory. Each reason connected to the outcome (failure to act). Secure: Both explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained, one named. Emerging: Reference to not acting without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Munich Agreement of September 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and up to 2 marks for specific supporting detail. Feature 1: Britain, France, Germany and Italy agreed to transfer the Sudetenland to Germany (1); Czechoslovakia was not consulted about the decision (1). Feature 2: Chamberlain returned to Britain claiming it secured 'peace for our time' (1); in March 1939 Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia, proving the agreement had failed (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the policy of appeasement failed to prevent the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Multiple causes explained — each concession encouraged further demands rather than satisfying Hitler; the Munich Agreement demonstrated that threats of force without follow-through were ineffective; Hitler's aims went beyond revising Versailles to continental domination; the Nazi-Soviet Pact removed the constraint of a two-front war. Secure: Two or more causes explained. Developing: One cause explained, others listed. Emerging: General statement about appeasement failing without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of the policy of appeasement. Interpretation A (the 'Guilty Men' view) argues Chamberlain and his colleagues made disastrous and avoidable mistakes by trusting Hitler. Interpretation B (the revisionist view) argues Chamberlain faced genuine constraints and made defensible decisions given the information available to him. How far do these interpretations differ and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear identification of key differences (moral verdict vs. contextual judgement; hindsight vs. contemporary knowledge); uses own knowledge (incomplete rearmament, public hostility to war, Munich concessions, March 1939 occupation) to support each; explains reasons for disagreement (era of writing, what evidence each weights). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Notes differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was appeasement the main cause of the Second World War? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs appeasement (Rhineland non-response, Munich) against other causes (Depression and rise of Nazism, Versailles grievances, Nazi-Soviet Pact, Hitler's ideology); engages with named interpretations ('Guilty Men', the revisionist defence of Chamberlain); reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: Clear argument addressing appeasement and at least two other factors with specific evidence. Developing: Some argument, possibly focused only on appeasement or only on Hitler. Emerging: Descriptive account of events. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. who they were, what they did, how they were authorised). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without clear detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Destroy the Four Olds Campaign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise detail (e.g. what the Four Olds were, specific targets attacked, role of Red Guards). Secure: Two features, each with some supporting detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons linked together (e.g. Mao's weakened position after the Great Leap Forward, fear of revisionism within the Party, Soviet example under Khrushchev). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Red Guards in the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of significance across criteria (scale of disruption, role in purging Party leaders, longer-term disillusionment among sent-down youth); counter-argument addressed. Secure: Clear argument about significance with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis. Emerging: Describes Red Guards with minimal argument about significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did Mao control the Cultural Revolution? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing Mao's control (planned targets, August 1966 rally, Down to the Countryside) against elements that escaped his control (Red Guard factionalism, Wuhan Incident, regional violence); specific evidence throughout. Secure: Clear argument with evidence; some attempt to weigh extent of control. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Cultural Revolution resulted in the deaths of Liu Shaoqi and other senior Party figures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (Mao's political strategy, removal of normal legal protections, role of Jiang Qing/Central Cultural Revolution Group, struggle session system). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Charles I's Personal Rule (1629-1640).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. Charles I levied ship money without parliamentary consent) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. originally a coastal tax, he extended it to inland counties in 1635; when John Hampden refused payment in 1637, the resulting court case attracted national attention and damaged Charles's image). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to Charles governing without Parliament. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Long Parliament's actions against royal power in 1640-41.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. the Long Parliament abolished ship money — removing Charles's main non-parliamentary revenue source; the Triennial Act 1641 required Parliament to meet at least every three years — making it impossible for any future monarch to rule without Parliament for an extended period). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I's attempt to arrest five Members of Parliament in January 1642 made civil war more likely.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (it was a constitutional outrage — using force against Parliament's members undermined the claim that Charles respected the rule of law; it failed — the MPs had been warned and escaped, humiliating the king; it confirmed parliamentary fears that Charles could not be trusted to keep agreements, making compromise impossible; it drove moderate MPs who had previously supported Charles into Parliament's camp, leaving him with a smaller royalist faction). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes the attempt without explaining why it accelerated war.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the execution of Charles I in 1649 was a significant turning point in the development of royal power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (it established the principle that monarchy was accountable — a king could be tried and executed for making war on his own people; it set a precedent no later monarch could ignore — even after the Restoration in 1660 the threat of violent removal was real; it demonstrated that Parliament, if sufficiently determined, could override even the most fundamental constitutional convention; the Restoration itself confirmed the change — Charles II had to accept parliamentary conditions and the abolished prerogatives were not restored). Secure: two factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: describes the execution as significant but does not explain the specific constitutional consequences. Emerging: describes the execution without addressing why it was a turning point.

practice_questions.text: How far did the period 1629-1660 permanently change the balance of power between the monarchy and Parliament? [You may consider: the Personal Rule; the execution of Charles I; the Restoration of 1660; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both the scale of change (execution of a king; prerogative courts abolished; ship money gone; Triennial Act; Restoration on parliamentary terms) and the limits of that change (monarchy restored in 1660; Cromwell himself dissolved Parliament and ruled personally; the Instrument of Government was a quasi-monarchical document; James II would soon challenge the settlement again). Overall judgement about how permanent the change was, anchored in specific evidence. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes the constitutional changes accurately but does not weigh their permanence. Emerging: narrative of events without addressing the question of change.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main events that led from the outbreak of the Civil War in 1642 to the execution of Charles I in 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points in sequence (Civil War breaks out 1642; Battle of Naseby 1645 — Parliamentarian victory; Charles surrenders to Scottish army 1646; Charles negotiates secretly with Scots 1647 — Second Civil War; Pride's Purge December 1648 removes moderate MPs; trial and execution of Charles I January 1649). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Parliament defeating Charles.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Nazi propaganda in the period 1933–1939.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the Volksempfänger cheap radio set was produced from 1933 and by 1938 reached approximately 70% of German households, enabling mass broadcast of Hitler's speeches). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Reich Chamber of Culture (1933).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. artists, writers, musicians and filmmakers had to join it in order to work, and Jews and political opponents were refused membership). Secure: Names a valid feature with some detail. Developing: States a feature without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Nazi propaganda was effective in maintaining popular support for the regime in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses multiple reasons — mass media penetration (radio, film, press), Nuremberg Rally spectacle, Hitler Myth concept (Kershaw), Volksgemeinschaft appealing to those scarred by class conflict, 1936 Olympics international image. Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why propaganda was so important to the Nazi regime between 1933 and 1939.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed methods with precise evidence (e.g. radio/Volksempfänger giving direct mass access; Nuremberg Rallies creating overwhelming spectacle; film/Riefenstahl constructing Hitler Myth; control of press through Reich Chamber). Analysis shows how each method functioned. Secure: Two methods with relevant evidence. Developing: Two methods with limited analysis. Emerging: One method or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of the Hitler Myth in maintaining the Nazi regime's popular support in the years 1933–1939?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs the Hitler Myth (Kershaw's concept — personal popularity surviving policy discontent) against other factors (terror, economic recovery, Volksgemeinschaft appeal, mass media). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Considers Hitler Myth and other factors with evidence. Developing: Describes the Hitler Myth without wider comparison. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that Nazi propaganda was the most important reason why the regime maintained popular support in the years 1933–1939. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument weighing propaganda (radio, film, press, rallies, Hitler Myth, Volksgemeinschaft) against other factors (terror making open opposition dangerous, economic recovery reducing unemployment, foreign policy successes creating national pride). Precise evidence; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Palmer Raids of 1919-1920.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: mass arrests of suspected radicals, often without warrants; around 10,000 people detained across 33 cities in the January 1920 raids; hundreds of foreign-born radicals deported to the Soviet Union.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Sacco and Vanzetti case became an international symbol of injustice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the judge’s public comments suggesting prejudice against the defendants’ anarchist beliefs undermined confidence in the fairness of the trial; the immigrants’ Italian background placed them at the intersection of anti-immigrant nativism and anti-radical hysteria, making it impossible to separate their trial from the political climate of the Red Scare). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the National Origins Act of 1924 was designed to restrict immigration from particular countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the deliberate use of the 1890 census (pre-mass-immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe) to calculate quotas, meaning the act was specifically designed to reduce immigration from Italy, Poland, and Russia while preserving British and Western European immigration; links this to nativist ideology, economic competition fears, and the post-war xenophobia that had produced the Red Scare; notes complete ban on Asian immigration. Secure: Two or more factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One factor explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the UNIA led by Marcus Garvey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: it promoted Black pride and African heritage; it promoted economic self-sufficiency through Black-owned businesses; it argued that African Americans should build an independent nation in Africa.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that nativism was the main cause of restrictions on immigration and civil liberties in 1920s America? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that assesses nativism alongside other causes (fear of Communism/anarchism from the Red Scare, economic competition, post-war anxiety); uses specific evidence for each (National Origins Act 1924 for nativism; Palmer Raids and Sacco and Vanzetti for Red Scare; Emergency Quota Act 1921 for economic pressure); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument addressing multiple causes with relevant evidence. Developing: Some awareness of multiple causes with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are given in this section.

practice_questions.text: Sources A and B give different views of the Red Scare in 1920s America. Source A says it was a genuine response to a real threat of Communist subversion. Source B says it was primarily a tool for targeting immigrants, minorities, and political dissenters. How far do the two sources agree? Use both sources and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (genuine security threat vs. manufactured hysteria, targeting criteria); tests both against own knowledge (post-Russian Revolution context, 1919 bombings for A; Palmer Raids abuses, Sacco and Vanzetti, deportation of thousands without evidence for B); explains why the two views differ (political perspective, evidence base, proximity to events). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Afrikaans Medium Decree of 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the decree AND gives a precise feature, e.g. it required half of all subjects in black secondary schools to be taught in Afrikaans; or students and teachers resisted it because Afrikaans was the language of the apartheid government. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to a language policy. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Soweto Uprising of June 1976.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the uprising AND gives a precise feature, e.g. about 20,000 students marched on 16 June 1976 and police opened fire, or Hector Pieterson was among the first killed. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to a student protest. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Soweto Uprising spread beyond Soweto after June 1976.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) students across South Africa shared the same grievances about Bantu Education and the Afrikaans decree; (2) Black Consciousness ideas had spread to black universities and townships nationwide; (3) the death of Biko in September 1977 intensified anger. Each reason with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Soweto Uprising weakened the apartheid regime.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed points — e.g. (1) international condemnation intensified, leading to a UN mandatory arms embargo in November 1977; (2) the uprising produced a new generation of ANC/MK recruits who would drive 1980s resistance. Each with specific evidence. Secure: Two points with good detail. Developing: One well-explained point. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the apartheid government's response to the Soweto Uprising failed to restore calm.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with precise evidence, e.g. force and mass detention gave protesters fresh grievances instead of removing the old ones; banning the Black Consciousness organisations in October 1977 did not stop young people leaving to join MK. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of the government's actions.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of young people in keeping resistance to apartheid alive in the period 1974–1979? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument about the significance of youth resistance (Soweto 1976, Soweto generation joining MK, Black Consciousness student organisations) weighed against other factors (Durban strikes and labour movement, ANC in exile, international pressure); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of Soweto with limited comparison. Emerging: Narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Olaudah Equiano's role in the British abolition movement.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Equiano published his autobiography in 1789 (1); it sold thousands of copies and provided first-person evidence of the experience of enslavement that was used by abolitionists to demonstrate the humanity of enslaved Africans (1). Feature 2: Equiano co-founded the Sons of Africa in the 1780s (1); this organisation wrote petitions to Parliament and organised campaigns working alongside white abolitionists such as Clarkson and Wilberforce (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Black communities grew in Britain during the eighteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons fully developed. Reason 1: The slave trade brought enslaved Africans to Britain as domestic servants with returning planters, merchants and naval officers; by mid-century, estimates suggest 10,000-15,000 Black people lived in Britain. Reason 2: The loss of the American colonies (1783) led to the evacuation of Black Loyalists who had fought for the Crown to Britain; this added another route of arrival distinct from the slavery system. Secure: Both reasons explained with evidence. Developing: One reason well explained. Emerging: General identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Somerset case of 1772 was significant but limited in its impact on slavery.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains what the ruling actually said (Somerset could not be forcibly removed from England) and what it did not say (it did not abolish slavery in England or the colonies); explains significance — it galvanised abolitionists, gave enslaved people a legal foothold, and was widely interpreted as ending slavery in England even though this was inaccurate; notes that slavery in the colonies continued unaffected until 1833. Secure: Explains both the significance and the limitation with evidence. Developing: Notes the importance of the case with some awareness of its limits. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which profits from the slave trade affected British society and built environment.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: slave-trade wealth funded the building of churches, country houses and public institutions in Bristol and Liverpool (2 marks); the triangular trade made Bristol and Liverpool major cities with global commercial networks (1-2 marks); banks and insurance companies were founded with slave-trade capital (1 mark). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that Black activists were more important than white campaigners in the abolition of the slave trade? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the contributions of the Sons of Africa (Equiano, Cugoano — petitions, public lectures, Equiano's autobiography) against white abolitionists (Clarkson's empirical research, Wilberforce's parliamentary campaigning, Sharp's legal work); recognises the coalition nature of the movement and the historical tendency to understate Black agency; considers that without Black testimony, the abolitionist case would have been weaker. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides. Developing: Some comparison with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the growth of the slave trade changed Black communities in Britain between 1672 and 1807.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two changes explained with causal analysis. Change 1: A free Black community developed alongside enslaved residents — as individual cases like Somerset's produced partial legal protections, formerly enslaved people gained freedom and formed networks that contributed to public and intellectual life. Change 2: Political organisation emerged — from isolated individuals like Sancho in the 1760s to the organised Sons of Africa in the 1780s, Black activists developed collective campaigning capacity. Secure: Two changes with relevant evidence. Developing: One change explained. Emerging: General statements.

practice_questions.text: Describe two difficulties the Wardens of the Marches faced in stopping border reiving.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. wardens were often from or allied with reiver families themselves, making impartial enforcement of border law difficult). Developing: vague (e.g. 'they were far away').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of border warfare on people living in the border region.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. repeated raids on farms took livestock, the main form of wealth; communities built peel towers as fortified refuges against attack. Developing: identifies impacts without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Union of Crowns (1603) was so effective in ending border reiving.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains how removing the frontier (which had sustained reiving by creating divided authority) allowed a joint commission to operate, how James systematically targeted major clans (Armstrongs), and why the speed of pacification reveals the political roots of the problem. Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Flodden (1513) was significant for Anglo-Scottish relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers immediate impact (James IV killed, Scottish nobility devastated), strategic significance (Scotland unable to raid effectively for a generation), and limits (border problem continued, Scottish alliance with France persisted). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Anglo-Scottish border remain ungovernable in the period c.1500–c.1603? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — balances evidence of persistence (reiving despite March Day system, Wardens compromised, peel towers as evidence of endemic threat) against evidence of partial order (March Days did function, Flodden showed English military reach) and the eventual rapid change post-1603; reaches a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument covering both sides. Developing: Mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why border warfare was connected to England's wider foreign policy during the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links the Auld Alliance (Scotland-France) to the two-front strategic problem for English kings; shows how Flodden (1513) coincided with Henry VIII's French campaign; connects Rough Wooing (1540s) to Tudor policy of forcing a Protestant union; explains how Elizabeth's support for Scottish Protestants eventually removed the threat. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Pilgrimage of Grace was a serious threat to Henry VIII.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. up to 40,000 people gathered under the banner of the Five Wounds, far more than the king could face in the field; the Pontefract Articles joined religious demands to social ones, so gentry as well as commons were drawn in. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the dissolution of the monasteries changed life for ordinary people.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. the poor lost the food and beds given at the monastery gate, which mattered most in the north where houses were the main source of relief; schools, hospitals and paid work went with the buildings. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Pilgrimage of Grace broke out in 1536.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons linked together (e.g. Suppression Act provoked religious anger + social grievances already present = large-scale rising). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason developed. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Pilgrimage of Grace failed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons linked (Henry's strategic delaying promises + lack of noble military commitment = rebels dispersed without securing concessions; second rising gave pretext for reprisals). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'The Pilgrimage of Grace shows how deeply ordinary people opposed the Reformation.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. In the exam this question comes with sources; here, answer from your own knowledge. Mastering: weighs the size of the rising and the religious demands of the Pontefract Articles against the social grievances in the same Articles, and against the many northerners who stayed at home; clear judgement. Secure: both sides argued with evidence. Developing: one side developed. Emerging: narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The dissolution of the monasteries harmed ordinary people more than it helped them.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Mastering: weighs the loss of poor relief, hospitality, schools and cultural treasures against gentry who bought land cheaply, towns that reused buildings and communities that welcomed the end of what they called idolatry; supported judgement. Secure: two groups compared with evidence. Developing: one group developed. Emerging: description.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the army carried out Pride's Purge in December 1648.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. the Presbyterian majority was still negotiating with Charles at Newport, so on 6 December 1648 Colonel Thomas Pride kept about 140 of them out and left a Rump willing to try the King. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the trial of Charles I in January 1649 was legally controversial.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons, e.g. the court was set up by the Rump alone after the Lords refused to take part, most of the appointed judges stayed away, and Charles refused to recognise its authority at all. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I's Engagement with the Scots made his execution more likely.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains how the Engagement (secret deal with Scots for Presbyterian settlement) led to the Second Civil War, how Preston made army hardliners determined there could be no settlement while Charles lived, and how this directly produced Pride's Purge and the decision to put him on trial. Secure: Two linked reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: The execution of Charles I in 1649 was inevitable once the Civil War began. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues against inevitability by showing multiple contingencies (Propositions of Newcastle 1646, Newport Treaty talks, Presbyterian majority opposition to execution) while explaining factors that made execution more likely over time (Engagement, Second Civil War, Pride's Purge). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides examined. Developing: One side mainly. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I refused to plead at his trial in January 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains constitutional argument (no court has jurisdiction over a king), religious conviction (divine right), strategic calculation (refusal undermined the court's legitimacy), precedent concern (accepting the court would destroy constitutional monarchy). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the army supported the execution of Charles I in 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the army's experience of the Second Civil War, sense of religious mission, Presbyterian Parliament's continued negotiations, conviction that Charles could not be trusted, Pride's Purge as expression of army will. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: Explain why London merchants were willing to lend the government 1.2 million pounds in 1694.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. the lenders were incorporated as the Bank of England in return; Parliament guaranteed the debt, so the loan was secure and the stock could be traded). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Indian textiles angered English weavers in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. Indian calicoes and muslins were cheaper and more fashionable than English cloth; weavers petitioned Parliament, which passed the Calico Acts of 1700 and 1721). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the founding of the Bank of England in 1694 was significant for England's military and commercial power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking the Bank of England to cheap borrowing, national debt, funding of war against France, and long-term commercial advantage with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one consequence explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: 'The East India Company mattered more than the Bank of England for Britain's commercial power in the period 1688–c.1730.' How far do you agree? Use Sources A and B [supplied in the exam] and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs both sides, uses precise evidence (the Kolkata trading post, Indian textiles and Chinese tea, set against the Bank of England, the national debt and Atlantic trade), works both sources into the argument, and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence and some use of the sources. Developing: Some argument; sources described rather than used. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence. Five of the 25 marks are for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why English merchants and the government saw the East India Company's trade as essential for national wealth.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the volume of Asian trade, the goods imported (textiles, tea, spices), the employment of joint-stock investment, and the generation of customs revenue, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why joint-stock companies suited long-distance trade in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. shareholders pooled capital that no single merchant could raise; risk was spread across many investors and shares could be sold on in London). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Black Panther Party's community programmes.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names a specific programme with accurate detail, e.g. the free breakfast programme fed up to 20,000 children per day across several US cities at its peak. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to the Panthers helping communities. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Malcolm X's political beliefs before 1964.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) Malcolm X rejected integration, arguing Black Americans should build separate institutions rather than seek admission to white society; (2) he rejected non-violence, arguing that Black people had the right to defend themselves 'by any means necessary' against attack. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Black Power emerged as a significant movement after 1965.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple causes with specific evidence — the Watts Riots (1965) revealed that the Civil Rights Act had not addressed the conditions of Northern urban Black Americans; SNCC's experience of violence in the South led some activists to question non-violence; King's gains had been legal rather than economic; Carmichael's 'Black Power' slogan crystallised a mood. Shows how these factors combined. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes Black Power without explaining its origins. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the FBI regarded the Black Panthers as a threat and used COINTELPRO against them.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) the Panthers' armed patrols monitoring police, combined with their nationalist ideology, led Hoover to call them the greatest internal security threat — COINTELPRO used surveillance and forged letters to generate internal conflict; (2) the Panthers' community programmes built a popular base that made them harder to marginalise politically, so the FBI used co-operation with local police in violent raids to physically destroy leadership. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was Malcolm X in the development of African American radical movements?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis covering his significance — provided an alternative framework to King that influenced Black Power and the Panthers; his autobiography shaped a generation; his break with the NOI and evolution toward internationalism showed the complexity of Black political thought. Places him in context: Black Power grew after his assassination; the Panthers cited his influence but developed independently; broader structural factors (Watts, Northern poverty) drove radicalism as much as any individual. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Malcolm X without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the development and impact of African American radical movements in the years 1965 to 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering Black Power (Carmichael, 1966), the Panthers (Newton, Seale; community programmes; COINTELPRO), the legacy of Malcolm X, the 1968 Olympic salute, and King's assassination. Reaches an integrated judgement about what the radical movements achieved and why they were suppressed. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several developments with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: share prices collapsed on Black Thursday, 24 October 1929, and on Black Tuesday, 29 October; the Dow Jones lost around a quarter of its value in two days; investors who had bought on margin were forced to sell.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Great Depression was so severe in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the banking crisis saw around 9,000 banks fail between 1930 and 1933, wiping out savings and cutting credit to businesses and families; the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 triggered retaliatory tariffs that caused world trade to shrink by about 65 per cent, meaning US exports collapsed at precisely the moment the economy needed demand). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Hoover's response to the Great Depression is described as 'too little, too late'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the ideological constraint (voluntary co-operation, refusal of direct federal relief) as well as specific policy failures (Smoot-Hawley made things worse; RFC was too small and too focused on businesses rather than unemployed individuals); uses the Bonus Army dispersal and the 1932 election result as evidence of political failure. Secure: Two or more factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One factor explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hoovervilles during the Great Depression.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: they were shantytowns built by homeless and unemployed Americans; they were made from scrap wood, cardboard and corrugated iron; the name blamed President Hoover for the crisis.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that Hoover's policies made the Great Depression worse? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges Hoover’s active interventions (RFC, public works) while arguing his ideological constraints (voluntary co-operation, refusal of direct relief) and policy mistakes (Smoot-Hawley) made the Depression significantly worse; uses specific evidence and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence across multiple policy areas. Developing: Some awareness of both actions and failures with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are given in this section.

practice_questions.text: Sources A and B give different views of Hoover's presidency during the Depression. Source A says he was a victim of circumstances beyond any president's control. Source B says his rigid ideology and policy mistakes significantly deepened the crisis. How far do the two sources agree? Use both sources and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (structural vs. individual blame, role of ideology, evidence base); tests both against own knowledge (global scale of Depression, bank failures for A; Smoot-Hawley, refusal of direct relief, Bonus Army for B); explains why the two views differ (political perspective, hindsight, evidence available). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the international sports boycott of apartheid South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the sports boycott AND gives a precise feature, e.g. South Africa was excluded from the Olympics from 1964; or the Gleneagles Agreement (1977) committed Commonwealth governments to discouraging sporting links. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to sports isolation. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the economic pressure placed on apartheid South Africa during the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names a form of economic pressure AND gives a precise feature, e.g. Chase Manhattan Bank refused to roll over South Africa's short-term loans in 1985, or the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986 was passed over President Reagan's veto. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to sanctions. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why international pressure on apartheid South Africa increased significantly during the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the State of Emergency and township revolt made the regime's brutality visible to global television audiences; (2) the Soweto uprising and Biko's death in 1977 had already created momentum for stronger action; (3) the ANC's external mission under Tambo successfully lobbied Western governments and the UN. Each reason with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Reagan and Thatcher opposed comprehensive sanctions against South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) 'constructive engagement' argument that economic ties would encourage gradual reform; (2) Cold War strategic concerns that sanctions would push South Africa towards instability that could benefit the Soviet Union. Present these as stated rationales that were contested, not as settled truths. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or one-sided answer.

practice_questions.text: Explain why sport became such an effective front in the campaign to isolate apartheid South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with precise evidence, e.g. white South Africans valued international sport highly, so exclusion from the Olympics after 1964 was felt personally; the Gleneagles Agreement of 1977 turned a public campaign into agreed policy across the Commonwealth. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: General comments about boycotts.

practice_questions.text: How far was international pressure the most important factor in forcing the apartheid government to negotiate in the late 1980s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing international pressure (sanctions, Chase Manhattan, Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act) against internal factors (UDF, State of Emergency, township revolt, Inkatha violence, economic costs of total strategy); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of sanctions with limited weighing against other factors. Emerging: Narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two agreements made at the Yalta Conference in February 1945.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each agreement scores 1 mark for identification and 1 for detail. Examples: Germany would be divided into four occupation zones (1) shared between the USA, Britain, France, and the USSR (1); Stalin pledged to hold free and unfettered elections in liberated Eastern European countries (1), including Poland (1); the Soviet Union agreed to enter the war against Japan (1) after Germany's defeat (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Potsdam Conference of July-August 1945 was more tense than the Yalta Conference.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed — Truman had replaced Roosevelt and was far less inclined to accommodate Stalin; the successful test of the atomic bomb gave the USA a new source of leverage and created new suspicion. Each with specific evidence and causal analysis. Secure: Both explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained, one named. Emerging: General reference to tension without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of Soviet 'salami tactics' in Eastern Europe 1945-1948.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and up to 2 marks for specific supporting detail. Feature 1: Coalition governments were progressively dismantled (1); non-communist parties and politicians were removed from power one at a time (1). Feature 2: The process culminated in a communist coup in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 (1); this was the last non-communist government in Eastern Europe to be removed (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why historians disagree about which side was more responsible for the origins of the Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that orthodox historians emphasise Soviet expansionism and broken Yalta pledges (using evidence such as salami tactics, Czech coup); revisionist historians emphasise US atomic diplomacy and dollar imperialism (using evidence such as atomic bomb use, Marshall Plan as economic pressure); post-revisionist historians acknowledge genuine security fears on both sides leading to misperception. Connects the different evidence bases to show why historians reach different conclusions. Secure: Two or more perspectives explained with evidence. Developing: One perspective explained, others named. Emerging: General statement about disagreement without content.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of who was responsible for the Cold War. Interpretation A (orthodox view) argues Soviet expansionism and broken Yalta pledges drove the breakdown. Interpretation B (revisionist view) argues US atomic diplomacy and economic power projection were equally or more responsible. How far do these interpretations differ and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (who is the primary actor, what evidence each selects); uses own knowledge (salami tactics vs. atomic bomb, Yalta pledges vs. Marshall Plan context) to support both; explains reasons for disagreement (Cold War era writing, access to archives, political context). Secure: Explains differences with relevant evidence. Developing: Notes differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was Soviet policy in Eastern Europe the main cause of the Cold War by 1948? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs Soviet actions (salami tactics, Czech coup, broken Yalta pledges) against US actions (atomic bomb, Truman's harder line at Potsdam, dollar diplomacy); engages with named schools (orthodox, revisionist, post-revisionist); reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: Clear argument addressing Soviet policy and at least one alternative cause with specific evidence. Developing: Some argument, may focus entirely on Soviet actions or entirely on the USA. Emerging: Descriptive account. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Act of Six Articles 1539 was a setback for reformers.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. it restored transubstantiation and clerical celibacy, undoing the drift of the Ten Articles; denying transubstantiation now carried death with no chance to take the words back, so Latimer and Shaxton gave up their bishoprics. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why religious change moved faster under Edward VI than under Henry VIII.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. Edward's regents, Somerset and then Northumberland, were reformers, so nothing held Cranmer back; the Chantries Act of 1547 and the Prayer Books of 1549 and 1552 struck at purgatory and at the Latin mass themselves, not just at Church government. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why religious policy under Henry VIII was inconsistent between 1536 and 1547.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons linked (Henry's personal conservatism on doctrine vs. reformers' influence through Cromwell + Cranmer; external political pressures). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple statement about change.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Book of Common Prayer changed English religious life.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons (English language enabling lay participation + theological shift on Eucharist in 1552); links to wider Reformation impact on clergy and parish life. Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: 'The English Bible changed religion in England more than any other measure before 1547.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. In the exam this question comes with sources; here, answer from your own knowledge. Mastering: weighs the Great Bible in every parish against the dissolution, the destruction of shrines and images, and the Six Articles, and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: two measures compared with evidence. Developing: one measure developed. Emerging: narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Worship in English parish churches was transformed between 1536 and 1552.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Mastering: weighs change (English services, the Prayer Books, whitewashed walls, chantries gone) against continuity (Henry kept Catholic doctrine, the north and west moved slowly, priests kept old habits); supported judgement. Secure: change and continuity argued with evidence. Developing: one side developed. Emerging: description.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Irish migration to England in the mid-nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Irish migrants concentrated in specific industrial cities (1); Liverpool, Manchester and London's East End became centres of Irish community life organised around Catholic parishes (1). Feature 2: Irish workers took the hardest and lowest-paid industrial jobs (1); they formed the core of the 'navvy' workforce building railways and canals (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Eastern European Jews came to Britain in large numbers between 1881 and 1914.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons fully developed. Reason 1: Push factor — the pogroms (state-tolerated antisemitic violence) that swept the Russian Empire from 1881 following Tsar Alexander II's assassination made life dangerous and unstable for Jewish communities in the Pale of Settlement. Reason 2: Pull factor — Britain had no immigration controls before 1905, was relatively politically stable, and London's East End offered established Jewish community networks and opportunities in the garment and trading industries. Secure: Both explained with evidence. Developing: One reason well explained. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Aliens Act of 1905 was historically significant.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains it was Britain's first peacetime immigration control — establishes the principle of state power to refuse entry; notes it was directed primarily at Eastern European Jewish refugees; explains it was driven by tabloid campaigns about overcrowding and 'alien influence'; notes the political exceptions that remained; discusses how it became the template for all later immigration legislation. Secure: Explains significance with at least two specific points. Developing: Describes the Act with some awareness of significance. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which Irish migrants contributed to British political movements in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: Feargus O'Connor edited the Northern Star (selling 50,000 copies weekly) and led the Chartist movement (1-2 marks); Irish radical traditions brought by migrants from a colonised country strengthened the democratic reform movement (1 mark); Irish Catholic parish and community networks gave migrants a base for organising in industrial cities (1 mark). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that migrant communities were primarily victims of hostility rather than active participants in British society? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument balancing evidence of hostility (anti-Irish discrimination, Aliens Act 1905 targeting Jews) against evidence of active participation and agency (O'Connor's Chartism, Match Girls Strike, Sons of Africa, Equiano's abolitionism, Huguenot industrial contribution); reaches a supported judgement about which characterisation is more accurate. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides. Developing: Some awareness of agency but mainly descriptive. Emerging: Lists examples of hostility without developed argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the passage of the Aliens Act (1905) represented a change in how Britain managed immigration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two changes explained causally. Change 1: Established state power to refuse entry — before 1905, anyone could enter Britain freely; the Act created the principle of border control for the first time in peacetime. Change 2: Created the category of the 'undesirable alien' — the state could now make value judgements about who was welcome; this became the template for the 1914 Status of Aliens Act and all later legislation. Secure: Two changes with evidence. Developing: One change explained. Emerging: General statements.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Bill of Rights (1689).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific restriction (e.g. it banned the crown from suspending laws without parliamentary consent) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. this was a direct response to James II's use of the Dispensing Power to bypass anti-Catholic legislation without consulting Parliament). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to limiting royal power. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why James II's actions in 1685-88 alarmed Parliament and the Church.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason. Mastering: two accurate reasons each with specific detail (e.g. James used his Dispensing Power to suspend anti-Catholic penal laws without parliamentary consent — directly overriding laws Parliament had passed; he ordered the Church of England to read his Declaration of Indulgence from every pulpit — using the Church as an instrument of Catholic policy against its will).
