Secure: both reasons with some development. Developing: one reason well described, one vague. Emerging: vague reference to James being Catholic.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Glorious Revolution of 1688 was significant for the development of parliamentary power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (the Bill of Rights (1689) formally listed what the Crown could not do without Parliament — banning the suspension of laws, standing armies and interference in elections; the Act of Settlement (1701) barred Catholics from the throne, making Parliament the arbiter of succession; William III's dependence on Parliament for war funding gave Parliament permanent financial leverage; the development of Walpole's Prime Ministerial role showed that governing Britain now required parliamentary management). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes 1688 as important without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Glorious Revolution was not 'glorious' from all perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (from a Catholic perspective, 1688 was the violent overthrow of the legitimate king by a foreign Protestant army — the Toleration Act excluded Catholics, the Act of Settlement barred them from the throne; from an Irish perspective, the Williamite Wars of 1689-91 caused significant military violence; from a Jacobite perspective, the legitimate Stuart succession had been broken by Parliamentary decision, not constitutional right — the 1715 and 1745 rebellions reflected this). Secure: two perspectives with some specific detail. Developing: describes one alternative perspective without explaining its basis in evidence. Emerging: vague reference to some people opposing James's removal.

practice_questions.text: How far did the events of 1688-1721 establish parliamentary sovereignty as the basis of British government? [You may consider: the Bill of Rights; the Act of Settlement; the Hanoverian succession; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both the establishment of parliamentary sovereignty (Bill of Rights restrictions; Act of Settlement made Parliament the arbiter of the throne; Triennial Act regularised Parliament; Walpole's Prime Ministerial role showed real power required parliamentary management) and its limits (the monarchy was still powerful; George III would try to reassert royal influence in the 1760s-80s; constituencies were unrepresentative — 'rotten boroughs'; most people still had no vote). Overall judgement required. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes the constitutional changes accurately but does not weigh the extent of parliamentary sovereignty achieved. Emerging: narrative of 1688 events without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main ways the Bill of Rights (1689) limited the power of the monarchy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points (banned suspension of laws without Parliament; banned peacetime standing army without Parliament; required free elections and free speech in Parliament; required regular Parliaments; made James II's Catholic successor arrangements invalid). Secure: two or three relevant points with supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to the Bill of Rights limiting royal power.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Four-Year Plan (1936).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the Four-Year Plan, launched in 1936 under Hermann Göring, aimed to make Germany self-sufficient and war-ready by 1940 by prioritising military production over consumer goods). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Strength Through Joy programme.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. it was run by the German Labour Front and gave workers subsidised holidays, concerts and cruises). Secure: Names a valid feature with some detail. Developing: States a feature without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Nazi economic recovery of the 1930s was not as beneficial for German workers as the unemployment figures suggest.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses multiple reasons — unemployment statistics excluded women, Jews and those on compulsory schemes; real wages stagnant or falling; loss of trade unions and collective bargaining; consumer goods sacrificed for rearmament; Volkswagen savings scheme never delivered. Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Nazi social and economic policies created winners and losers in German society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed points with precise evidence identifying who gained (big business, armaments producers, some farmers initially, Hitler Youth participants) and who lost (workers losing unions, women pressured out of work, Mittelstand squeezed by war economy, Jewish workers excluded). Secure: Two points with relevant evidence. Developing: Two points with limited analysis. Emerging: One point or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant was rearmament in shaping the experiences of different groups within German society in the years 1933–1939?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses rearmament's impact across multiple groups (workers losing real wages as consumer goods were sacrificed; big business gaining contracts; farmers pressured for food self-sufficiency; women recalled into workforce despite ideology) and assesses relative significance against other factors (propaganda, terror, social welfare initiatives). Secure: Considers rearmament's impact and compares with other factors. Developing: Describes rearmament without comparative analysis. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that Nazi economic policy benefited most German people in the years 1933–1939. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument: genuine benefits (falling unemployment, Strength Through Joy, Hitler Youth, rearmament creating jobs) set against costs and limitations (loss of unions, manipulated statistics, real wage stagnation, policy failures for Mittelstand and farmers, Four-Year Plan's consumer sacrifice). Precise evidence; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell's campaign in Ireland in 1649 is still remembered so bitterly.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. about 3,500 died when Drogheda was stormed in September 1649, between 1,500 and 2,000 died at Wexford the next month, and the conquest was followed by land confiscation and transplantation. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Rump Parliament passed the Navigation Act in 1651.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons, e.g. the Act forced imports into English ships or ships of the producing country in order to strike at the Dutch carrying trade and build up English commerce; it helped bring on the First Anglo-Dutch War of 1652-54. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell dissolved the Rump Parliament in April 1653.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons (Rump refused to hold elections, blocked godly reform, sat too long, narrow self-interest) linked with analysis of the deeper tension between army mission and parliamentary authority. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Cromwell's military campaigns in Ireland (1649) were justified. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument considering Cromwell's own justification (laws of war, 1641 rebellion), evidence from Drogheda and Wexford (documented death tolls), contemporary norms of siege warfare, and the specific circumstances at Wexford where soldiers acted without orders. Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Considers both sides with evidence. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell won the Battle of Dunbar in September 1650.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Cromwell's military skill, Scottish Presbyterian ministers' decision to purge 'ungodly' officers before the battle, Scottish army manoeuvred into unfavourable terrain, numerical disadvantage overcome by discipline. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the relationship between the Rump Parliament and Cromwell became increasingly difficult 1649–1653.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains different views of the republic's purpose (Parliament's narrow interest vs army's godly mission), Rump's refusal to dissolve, blocking of legal reform, army's frustration after military victories, leading to dissolution. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: Explain the part the Royal African Company played in the slave trade before 1698.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. chartered in 1672 under the Duke of York, it held a royal monopoly on English trade with West Africa; it transported an estimated 100,000 enslaved Africans between 1672 and 1713). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) mattered for Britain's slave trade.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. it ended the War of the Spanish Succession; it gave Britain the Asiento, a 30-year contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies, which went to the South Sea Company). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the lifting of the Royal African Company's monopoly in 1698 had such significant consequences for the slave trade.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking the Ten Per Cent Act to open competition, the dramatic rise in enslaved Africans transported (estimated 470,000 in 1700–1730), and the embedding of the slave trade across British commercial society. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one consequence explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: 'The slave economy was the main reason for Britain's commercial growth in the period 1688–c.1730.' How far do you agree? Use Sources A and B [supplied in the exam] and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs both sides, uses precise evidence (sugar profits, the slave ports, the Asiento, set against the East India Company and the Bank of England, and weighed with the human cost), works both sources into the argument, and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence and some use of the sources. Developing: Some argument; sources described rather than used. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence. Five of the 25 marks are for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the South Sea Bubble (1720) showed the dangers of linking state finance to the slave trade.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the South Sea Company's assumption of national debt, speculative inflation of its share price due to expectations of Asiento profits, the crash when reality fell short, and Robert Walpole's subsequent management. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Explain what conditions on the Middle Passage were like for enslaved Africans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. extreme overcrowding below decks; mortality of roughly 10 to 25 per cent per voyage from dysentery, smallpox, dehydration and deliberate violence). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways the New Model Army was more effective than earlier Parliamentary forces.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. the New Model Army was a national force paid regularly and promoted by merit rather than birth, making it more reliable and disciplined than county-based militias). Developing: vague (e.g. 'it was better trained').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the civil wars on ordinary people in England.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. Parliamentary weekly assessment imposed the heaviest taxation England had ever seen; soldiers quartered in homes consumed food and seized livestock and horses. Developing: identifies impacts without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell's campaign in Ireland (1649–50) was so significant.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers military significance (reconquest of Ireland), immediate human cost (Drogheda, Wexford), and long-term consequences (land confiscations, Catholic dispossession, reshaping of Irish society). Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Wars of the Three Kingdoms began in Scotland rather than England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links Charles I's imposition of the prayer book to Scottish resistance, the Bishops' Wars, and how Scottish military pressure forced Charles to recall Parliament, which then used his weakness to challenge his power. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the civil wars of 1642–51 transform British society? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers political transformation (execution of Charles I, republic, Commonwealth), military change (New Model Army), economic impact (taxation, land confiscation in Ireland), human cost, and elements of continuity (monarchy restored 1660, many pre-war social structures survived in England); reaches a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument covering transformation and continuity. Developing: Mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Naseby (1645) was a decisive turning point in the English Civil War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains why the New Model Army's discipline was decisive (cavalry reform, national force, meritocratic command), the strategic consequences (King's main army destroyed, correspondence captured), and how this led to Charles's capture. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Mao personality cult during the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. mass publication of the Little Red Book, Tiananmen rallies, Mao badges). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without specific detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Communist propaganda during the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise supporting detail (e.g. Party press, thought reform sessions, model campaigns). Secure: Two features, each with some detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Mao personality cult was important to the success of the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons with specific evidence (e.g. how the cult gave Mao authority to override normal Party structures, role of Lin Biao, how it silenced potential opponents). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Communist propaganda in maintaining CCP control during the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of significance (immediate social control, long-term impact on intellectual life, how Lin Biao's death undermined it); counter-argument considered. Secure: Clear argument with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis of why significant. Emerging: Describes propaganda with minimal argument.

practice_questions.text: How far did the CCP successfully control the people of Tibet between 1950 and 1976? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence of control (military incorporation, end of theocracy, Cultural Revolution destruction) against resistance (1959 uprising, Dalai Lama's exile, continued religious identity); both PRC and exile/Western framings acknowledged. Secure: Clear argument with evidence; some attempt to weigh extent of control. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the death of Lin Biao in 1971 was damaging for the CCP's propaganda.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (Lin's role in building the cult, the contradiction of denouncing a praised leader, public loss of confidence in official claims). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Great Reform Act (1832).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific reform (e.g. it abolished rotten boroughs) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. Old Sarum had seven voters and two MPs; the Act removed such constituencies and redistributed their seats to new industrial towns like Manchester and Birmingham). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to increasing the electorate. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the campaign for women's suffrage.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features clearly distinguishing between suffragist and suffragette tactics (e.g. the NUWSS under Millicent Fawcett used constitutional lobbying and peaceful petition — a non-violent strategy of persuading Parliament; the WSPU under Emmeline Pankhurst used militant direct action including arson attacks and hunger strikes — designed to make the political cost of continued refusal too high). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague or confusing the two organisations. Emerging: vague reference to women protesting.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Great Reform Act (1832) was a limited reform.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (it extended the vote only to men with property worth £10/year in boroughs — leaving most working-class men unrepresented; there was still no secret ballot, leaving tenants vulnerable to landlord pressure; no women were enfranchised; the electorate grew from about 400,000 to 650,000 — still a tiny fraction of the population; the principle of property as the franchise qualification was retained, not abolished). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes the Act accurately but does not explain why it was limited.

practice_questions.text: Explain why women gained the vote in 1918 rather than earlier.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains two or more factors that made 1918 the moment (women's war work in munitions, nursing and transport made their civic contribution impossible to ignore; the WSPU suspended militancy during the war, making a hostile government response less defensible; the 1918 Act was partly driven by the need to enfranchise servicemen — women's inclusion became politically viable at the same moment; constitutional campaigning by the NUWSS had built sustained parliamentary support over decades). Considers why earlier attempts failed. Secure: two factors with some specific evidence. Developing: one factor developed or two undeveloped. Emerging: simply states that women worked in the war without explaining the political connection.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Reform Acts of 1832-1884 represent a genuine transfer of power to the people? [You may consider: rotten boroughs; the extension of the franchise; women's suffrage; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument acknowledging both real change (abolition of rotten boroughs; towns represented for first time; working-class urban then rural men enfranchised; electorate grew from 400,000 to c.5 million 1832-1885) and significant continuity (property qualification retained; no secret ballot until 1872; no women enfranchised; most working-class men still excluded in 1867; 'transfer of power to the people' only complete in 1928 with equal franchise). Overall judgement required. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes reforms accurately but does not weigh the extent of power transfer. Emerging: narrative of reform acts without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main differences between the suffragist and suffragette campaigns for votes for women.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific comparative points (NUWSS vs WSPU; Fawcett vs Pankhurst; constitutional lobbying vs militant direct action; petitions and meetings vs arson and hunger strikes; NUWSS supported the war effort throughout; WSPU suspended militancy 1914; Sylvia Pankhurst split from WSPU over the war). Secure: two or three accurate comparative points. Developing: one point of comparison, or describes one organisation only. Emerging: vague reference to different tactics.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Britain's treatment of Jewish refugees in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The British government's visa system was restrictive (1); many German Jews who applied for entry were refused, and thousands later perished in the Holocaust (1). Feature 2: Some individuals and organisations worked to bring refugees to safety (1); Nicholas Winton privately organised the rescue of 669 Czech children in 1939 as part of the Kindertransport scheme (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why British attitudes towards refugees in the 1930s were mixed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons developed with specific evidence. Reason 1: Economic anxiety — with Britain still recovering from the Depression, some politicians and newspapers argued Jewish refugees would compete for scarce jobs; government ministers cited fears of public opposition. Reason 2: Antisemitism — documented antisemitic attitudes in parts of British society and government meant Jewish refugees were not always seen as deserving of sympathy; some newspaper coverage framed refugees as a burden. Secure: Both reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason explained. Emerging: General identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Kindertransport is considered both a humanitarian success and an illustration of the limits of British generosity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains success — approximately 10,000 children brought to safety, Nicholas Winton's private efforts, organised by charitable networks; and limits — adults were excluded, most parents perished, the scheme operated on expectation of eventual return, children grew up separated from families in complex situations. Connects this to broader government reluctance to admit more Jewish refugees. Secure: Explains both aspects with evidence. Developing: Explains one aspect well. Emerging: Describes the scheme without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the 1914-18 war changed how Britain treated its migrant communities.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: Status of Aliens Act 1914 required all foreign nationals to register with police and gave government powers of internment (1-2 marks); long-term German and Austro-Hungarian residents were interned despite decades of settlement (1 mark); 1919 race riots showed Black and Asian workers faced violence after demobilisation (1-2 marks). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that wartime Britain was hostile to all migrant communities? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument noting variation — Belgian refugees received substantial sympathy and support in 1914-18; Polish veterans were welcomed in principle via the 1947 Act; but German internees, Black and Asian workers (1919 riots), and Jewish refugees faced hostility. Argues that reception was contingent on perceived loyalty, race, and economic context rather than uniformly hostile. Engages with specific examples drawn from across the period. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from at least two communities. Developing: Some comparative points. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the experience of Polish veterans after 1945 illustrates tensions in post-war British society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two tensions explained causally. Tension 1: Economic competition — trade unions feared Polish workers would undercut wages in post-war austerity conditions; despite the Polish Resettlement Act, Polish veterans faced hostility in some industries. Tension 2: Identity and loyalty — Polish veterans had strong claims to British gratitude for their wartime service (RAF Battle of Britain squadrons), yet were depicted in some press as economic migrants; this reveals how even demonstrable wartime contribution did not guarantee welcome. Secure: Two tensions explained. Developing: One tension explained. Emerging: General descriptions.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Delano grape strike led by Cesar Chavez.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the strike and gives specific detail, e.g. Chavez organised a national consumer boycott of California grapes; by 1968 an estimated 17 million Americans were boycotting grapes, forcing growers to negotiate. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to a farmworkers' strike. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the American Indian Movement (AIM) in the years 1968 to 1973.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) AIM was founded in Minneapolis in 1968 to monitor police violence against Native Americans in urban areas, influenced by Black Power; (2) in 1973 AIM members occupied Wounded Knee for 71 days in a standoff with federal agents, protesting treaty violations and reservation conditions. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Chicano civil rights movement drew on similar tactics to the African American civil rights movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — Chavez consciously modelled his approach on King's non-violent direct action (marches, fasting, boycotts); the Brown v Board precedent showed courts could be used; the Civil Rights Act opened possibilities for Title VII employment claims; both movements faced similar structural discrimination. Shows the connection between the movements. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes the tactics without explaining the connection. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Wounded Knee occupation of 1973 was significant for Native American civil rights.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) the 71-day occupation brought national media attention to treaty violations and reservation poverty that had been largely ignored; (2) it demonstrated AIM's ability to organise a sustained confrontation with federal authorities, showing the scale of Native American grievance and building movement solidarity. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant were the campaigns of Cesar Chavez and the UFW in improving the lives of Chicano Americans?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis covering gains (union recognition for farmworkers in 1970; national consumer boycott demonstrated Latino political power; inspired wider Chicano movement) and limits (farmworkers remained among the poorest workers; UFW membership later declined; broader housing and educational inequality unchanged). Compares UFW's significance to other parts of the Chicano movement and to Native American campaigns. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Chavez without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the impact of civil rights campaigns for Native Americans and Chicanos in the years 1962 to 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering both groups — UFW, grape boycott, union victory (Chicano); AIM, Alcatraz, Trail of Broken Treaties, Wounded Knee, Indian Civil Rights Act (Native American). Reaches an integrated judgement about what changed and what remained limited, comparing the two movements. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several developments with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited structure or covers only one group. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Nuremberg Laws (1935).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jews of German citizenship, depriving them of civil rights, and the companion law banned marriage between Jews and non-Jewish Germans). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. on 9–10 November 1938 around 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps). Secure: Names a valid feature with some detail. Developing: States a feature without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 were a significant turning point in Nazi persecution of Jews.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses multiple reasons — stripped citizenship creating legal basis for discrimination; banned intermarriage separating Jews from German society; defined Jewishness racially creating an inescapable category; enabled further escalation of persecution. Placed in context of earlier measures and what followed. Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why effective opposition to the Nazi regime was so limited in the years 1933–1939.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. destruction of KPD/SPD organisations in 1933 removing the political opposition base; Gestapo and denunciation system making underground activity very dangerous; churches focused on institutional autonomy not political opposition; T4 protest example showing what was required for effectiveness). Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: Two reasons with limited analysis. Emerging: One reason or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the persecution of Jewish people in comparison with the persecution of other groups in Nazi Germany in the years 1933–1939?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs the scale and systematic nature of Jewish persecution (Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht, emigration pressure) against parallel persecution of Roma (racial aliens), disabled people (Sterilisation Law, T4), homosexuals (Paragraph 175), Jehovah's Witnesses. Argues whether Jewish persecution was uniquely significant or part of a broader racial ideology. Secure: Compares Jewish and other group persecution with specific evidence. Developing: Describes one group in detail without comparison. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that religious opposition was the most significant form of resistance to the Nazi regime in Germany in the years 1933–1939. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument weighing religious opposition (Confessing Church, Niemöller, Bonhoeffer, von Galen on T4) against other forms (Communist underground, individual acts of courage, youth subcultures, Mittelstand economic grievances). Assesses the effectiveness and limitations of each. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the risings of 1549 in Norfolk and the south-west had different causes.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. the western rebels' Articles demand the Latin mass and the return of the Six Articles, so religion drove them; Kett's rebels camped outside Norwich over the enclosure of common land. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why responses to the Reformation differed from one English parish to another.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. London and the south-east had heard evangelical preaching since the 1520s, so many parishes welcomed the changes; in the north and west priests kept older practices quietly, and royal visitors could not be everywhere. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Prayer Book Rebellion broke out in Devon and Cornwall in 1549.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons linked (imposition of English service where Cornish was still spoken + loss of Latin mass = direct attack on familiar devotional life; rebels' Articles show clearly religious motivation). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the government was able to defeat the Prayer Book Rebellion.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons (professional military force vs. armed civilians; rebels isolated geographically; Somerset's government willing to use extreme force). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: 'The Prayer Book Rebellion shows that most English people rejected the Reformation.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. In the exam this question comes with sources; here, answer from your own knowledge. Mastering: weighs the depth of feeling in Devon and Cornwall against quiet acceptance elsewhere, outward conformity, and towns that welcomed reform; clear judgement. Secure: both sides argued with evidence. Developing: one side developed. Emerging: narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Resistance never seriously threatened the Reformation in England between 1536 and 1549.' How far do you agree? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Mastering: weighs the size of the Pilgrimage of Grace and the Prayer Book Rebellion against their defeat, the lack of noble leadership and the government's willingness to use force; supported judgement. Secure: two risings compared with evidence. Developing: one rising developed. Emerging: description.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways the 1745 Jacobite Rising threatened the government more than the 1715 Rising.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. Charles Edward Stuart's army advanced as far as Derby in December 1745, just 125 miles from London, causing panic in the capital, whereas the 1715 rising never reached England's heartland). Developing: vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the repression that followed the Battle of Culloden (1746).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. Disarming Act (1746) banned Highland dress and weapons; Heritable Jurisdictions Act (1747) abolished the power of clan chiefs to hold their own courts, breaking clan authority. Developing: identifies impacts without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Seven Years War (1756–63) was significant for Britain's imperial power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains Pitt's strategy (naval supremacy, colonial focus), decisive victories (Plains of Abraham, Quiberon Bay), Treaty of Paris gains (Canada, India), and long-term significance (dominant global power, model for future British grand strategy). Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Highland Clearances were a consequence of the Jacobite defeat at Culloden.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links Culloden defeat to repression (Disarming Act, Heritable Jurisdictions Act), explains how this stripped clan chiefs of power, and then connects to economic pressures that drove evictions and conversion to sheep farming; notes long-term impact on Highland population. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the wars of the eighteenth century transform Britain's place in the world? Explain your answer with reference to the Jacobite risings and the Seven Years War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers internal transformation (end of Jacobite threat, Highland integration into British identity) and external transformation (Seven Years War imperial gains, naval dominance, global power status) with elements of continuity (debt, Parliamentary pressure, social structures); reaches a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument covering both internal and external dimensions. Developing: Mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Culloden (1746) was the last pitched battle fought on British soil.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains military factors (artillery, musket fire), the nature of the Jacobite defeat (no further viable force), the subsequent repression breaking clan military capacity, and the longer-term pacification of the Highlands. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why coffee houses became important in early eighteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. Lloyd's coffee house became the centre of marine insurance; newspapers were read aloud in them, so political opinion formed outside Parliament). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain how everyday life in Britain changed because of the consumer revolution, 1688–c.1730.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed changes with precise evidence (e.g. sugar consumption per head rose above that of any other European country; tea moved from an aristocratic luxury to a middle-class staple). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one change. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ordinary British people were more widely involved in the slave trade than is sometimes assumed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation covering slave ports, supply industries, investment, consumer demand for slave-produced goods, with precise evidence (Bristol, Liverpool statistics, Lloyd's). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one dimension explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: 'The consumer revolution changed British society more than any other effect of empire in the period 1688–c.1730.' How far do you agree? Use Sources A and B [supplied in the exam] and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs both sides, uses precise evidence (diet, coffee houses and press culture, set against the slave ports, racial ideology and the constitutional changes of the same years), works both sources into the argument, and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence and some use of the sources. Developing: Some argument; sources described rather than used. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence. Five of the 25 marks are for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why racial hierarchy ideas developed in Britain during this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the ideological function of racial hierarchy in justifying the slave trade, its impact on settled Black communities in Britain, and the legal ambiguity of their status. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Explain what forms early opposition to the slave trade took in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. Quaker meetings began to condemn the slave trade formally from 1727; enslaved people resisted through plantation rebellions and, in Britain, through the courts). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Outline two consequences of the Truman Doctrine for Cold War relations in Europe.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed consequences, each with a specific supporting detail (e.g. containment policy formalised; Western bloc consolidation accelerated). Secure: Two identified consequences with some development. Developing: Two consequences identified but not developed beyond a basic statement. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the USSR rejected the Marshall Plan.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, each with specific factual support and a clear link to the question (e.g. Stalin feared economic dependency on the USA; Cominform used to enforce rejection on Eastern bloc states). Secure: Two reasons developed with some supporting detail. Developing: Two reasons identified but development is limited or repetitive. Emerging: One basic reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Berlin Airlift was a significant turning point in the early Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument for significance with specific evidence (323-day duration; 45-second landing intervals; Soviet climbdown) linked clearly to changed Cold War dynamics. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail but less developed analysis. Developing: Some explanation with limited detail. Emerging: Brief descriptive points.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Berlin Blockade 1948–1949.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features, each supported by specific accurate detail (e.g. Stalin closed road, rail and canal routes; the blockade lasted 323 days). Secure: Two features with some supporting detail. Developing: Two features identified but without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the USA introduced the Marshall Plan in 1947.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes linked to the Marshall Plan's purpose, with specific supporting detail and causal analysis (economic: preventing communist expansion in war-weakened states; political: undercutting Soviet influence). Secure: Two causes developed with relevant detail. Developing: One cause developed or two causes with limited development. Emerging: Simple statement of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Germany was divided into two states by 1949.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation identifying multiple causal factors (post-war Allied disagreement, introduction of Deutschmark, Berlin Blockade) linked coherently. Specific detail required. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Some explanation but development limited. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Democracy Wall movement of 1978–79.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. location, type of content posted, Wei Jingsheng's essay). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without clear detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Gang of Four trial of 1980–81.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise detail (e.g. who was tried, Jiang Qing's conduct, sentences passed, political purpose of the trial). Secure: Two features, each with some detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Deng Xiaoping suppressed the Democracy Wall movement in 1979.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (Deng had consolidated power at the Third Plenum; wall had served its tactical purpose; Wei's demands threatened one-party rule; distinction between economic and political reform). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Tiananmen Incident of 1976 for the succession struggle after Mao.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis across criteria (how it temporarily weakened Deng, how it demonstrated public disillusionment with the radical left, role in Gang of Four's downfall); counter-argument considered. Secure: Clear argument with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis. Emerging: Describes events with minimal argument about significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did the death of Mao in 1976 lead to a fundamental change in China's political system? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence of change (Gang of Four arrested, Third Plenum reform agenda, limited political openness) against continuity (one-party rule, suppression of Democracy Wall, Wei Jingsheng imprisoned); specific evidence throughout; balanced conclusion. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides; some weighing. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Gang of Four were arrested so quickly after Mao's death.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (Hua Guofeng's political interests, military commanders' support, popular antipathy to Cultural Revolution excesses, Gang's lack of military base). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two agencies created during Roosevelt's Hundred Days in 1933.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct agency, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: the CCC, which employed young unemployed men in conservation work; the TVA, which built dams and supplied electricity across seven Southern states; the AAA, which paid farmers to cut production; FERA, which gave grants to states for relief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Second New Deal (1935) went further than the First New Deal.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both ways fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the Wagner Act created legally enforceable rights for workers to join unions, going well beyond the NRA’s voluntary codes; the Social Security Act established the first federal safety net — old-age pensions and unemployment insurance — whereas the First New Deal had focused on emergency relief rather than permanent social provision). Secure: Both ways explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Tennessee Valley Authority was significant.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance in multiple dimensions — it brought electricity to seven previously impoverished Southern states; provided flood control along the Tennessee River; created construction and long-term employment; and represented an ideological shift (government directly owning and operating a major utility, which conservatives attacked as socialism). Secure: Two or more dimensions explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One dimension explained, others named. Emerging: General statement about importance without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Social Security Act of 1935.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: it created federal old-age pensions for workers over 65; it set up a joint federal-state unemployment insurance system; it was funded by payroll taxes shared between employer and employee; it excluded domestic servants and farm labourers.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the New Deal transformed American society? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges transformations (scale of federal intervention, Wagner Act rights, Social Security system, TVA electrification) while explaining limits (NRA struck down; Social Security excluded domestic servants and farm labourers; unemployment still high at 14% in 1937; court-packing plan failed); uses specific evidence and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument across multiple dimensions of change and its limits. Developing: Some awareness of both with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are given in this section.

practice_questions.text: Sources A and B give different views of the New Deal. Source A says it saved American democracy and capitalism by demonstrating that government could manage economic crises. Source B says it was a confused improvisation that failed to end the Depression and preserved racial inequality. How far do the two sources agree? Use both sources and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (success/failure in ending Depression, ideological coherence, racial justice); tests both against own knowledge (Wagner Act, SSA, TVA for A; NRA struck down, African Americans excluded, unemployment still high 1937 for B); explains why the two views differ (political perspective, time of writing, evidence base). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the United Democratic Front (UDF) founded in 1983.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the UDF AND gives a precise feature, e.g. it united over 400 organisations including trade unions, church groups and civic bodies; or it explicitly aligned with the ANC's Freedom Charter. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to an anti-apartheid coalition. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the national State of Emergency declared in June 1986.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the State of Emergency AND gives a precise feature, e.g. the security forces could detain people without charge, or about 30,000 people were held at its peak. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to emergency powers. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Tricameral Parliament of 1983 provoked such strong resistance from black South Africans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) it excluded black South Africans entirely while giving Coloured and Indian communities separate chambers — seen as a divide-and-rule tactic; (2) it signalled that Botha's 'total strategy' was reform without fundamentally changing white minority rule. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the apartheid regime faced both internal and external crisis by the mid-1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) township revolt and the UDF had made large areas ungovernable; (2) Chase Manhattan's loan refusal in 1985 and the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act 1986 created a financial emergency. Secure: Two reasons with good detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the conflict between Inkatha and the ANC in the 1980s was not simply an ethnic quarrel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with precise evidence, e.g. the Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that state security forces armed Inkatha in secret; the two movements also split over sanctions and the armed struggle, which are political questions rather than ethnic ones. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of the violence.

practice_questions.text: How far was the State of Emergency (1985–1990) an effective response by P.W. Botha's government to the challenge of the UDF and township revolt? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing effectiveness (suppressed visible protest, detained thousands, censored media) against limitations (did not resolve political crisis, damaged economic confidence, increased international isolation, did not destroy UDF); reaches a supported judgement about 'how far'. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of State of Emergency with limited analysis of effectiveness. Emerging: Narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Instrument of Government was an unusual constitution for England.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. it was England's first and only written constitution, army officers wrote it in December 1653, and it made Cromwell Lord Protector sharing executive power with a Council of State. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Rule of the Major-Generals became so unpopular.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons, e.g. eleven military districts put army officers in charge of ordinary government, a 10% tax fell on Royalist incomes, and the Major-Generals closed alehouses and stopped horse racing and bear-baiting. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell refused the crown offered by the Humble Petition and Advice in 1657.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Cromwell's theological reasoning (God had blasted the title of king), his reliance on providentialist thinking, army opposition to kingship, and the practical constitutional provisions he accepted instead. Links these together. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple answer.

practice_questions.text: The Protectorate (1653–1658) successfully solved the problem of governing England after the Civil War. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing achievements (stability, foreign policy, religious toleration) against failures (no lasting constitutional settlement, each Parliament challenged the Instrument, Major-Generals unpopular, collapse after Cromwell's death). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides examined. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Barebone's Parliament dissolved itself in December 1653.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (radical proposals to abolish tithes and common law, moderate members alarmed, fear of social revolution, army concern about stability) with linked argument. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Rule of the Major-Generals was ended in 1657.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains parliamentary opposition (resentment of military rule, Puritan interference in daily life, 10% tax on Royalists), broad unpopularity, and Cromwell's need for parliamentary support for his foreign policy. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways Florence Nightingale's work in the Crimean War changed the British Army.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. Nightingale used statistical analysis to demonstrate the link between hospital sanitation and mortality rates at Scutari, which led to improved conditions that dramatically reduced deaths from disease). Developing: vague (e.g. 'she was a good nurse').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the Second Boer War on British society.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. concentration camp deaths (c.26,000 Boer civilians) became a major political scandal that undermined public support for the war; the poor physical fitness of recruits contributed to Liberal welfare reforms addressing working-class health. Developing: identifies features without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Crimean War was significant in changing the British Army.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers military failures (supply breakdown, Charge of the Light Brigade, disease deaths), Nightingale's nursing reforms and statistical methods, Mary Seacole's contribution, and the subsequent professionalisation of army medicine. Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Peterloo Massacre (1819) can be seen as a consequence of the Napoleonic Wars.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links demobilisation (unemployment, poverty), Corn Laws (bread prices kept high), use of wartime cavalry culture against domestic crowds, and the government's instinct to suppress dissent as it had suppressed external enemies. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the wars of the nineteenth century improve the lives of ordinary British people? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — balances improvements (nursing reform after Crimea, welfare reforms driven by Boer War fitness crisis, national pride from Trafalgar and Waterloo) against costs (taxation, Peterloo, demobilisation poverty, concentration camp scandal); reaches a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument covering both sides. Developing: Mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Trafalgar (1805) was significant for Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains military significance (ended French invasion threat, confirmed naval supremacy), cultural significance (Nelson's death and national mourning), and longer-term significance (naval dominance underpinned 19th-century empire). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the CODESA negotiations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names CODESA AND gives a precise feature, e.g. the ANC's chief negotiator was Cyril Ramaphosa and the government's was Roelf Meyer; or CODESA produced an Interim Constitution agreed in November 1993. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to negotiations. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of F.W. de Klerk's speech of 2 February 1990.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the speech AND gives a precise feature, e.g. he unbanned the ANC, PAC and SACP, or he announced that Nelson Mandela would be released. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to reform. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why F.W. de Klerk decided to unban the ANC and enter negotiations in 1990.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the combination of economic crisis (Chase Manhattan, sanctions) and internal unrest had left the regime in an unsustainable position; (2) the failure of 'total strategy' in Angola (Cuito Cuanavale, Tripartite Accord) had undermined military confidence. Each reason with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the negotiations between the ANC and the apartheid government were nearly derailed in 1992–1993.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the Boipatong massacre (June 1992) killed 45 people and the ANC alleged security force complicity, withdrawing from talks; (2) the assassination of Chris Hani (April 1993) provoked mass anger that threatened violent breakdown. Secure: Two reasons with good detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the fighting at Cuito Cuanavale in 1987–88 weakened the apartheid government's total strategy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with precise evidence, e.g. the SADF could not win a clear victory and took heavy casualties, which broke the promise that military force could hold the region; South Africa then signed the Tripartite Accord in December 1988 and pulled out of Angola and Namibia. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of the battle.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of F.W. de Klerk in bringing apartheid to an end? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing de Klerk's significance (unbanning, Mandela release, CODESA leadership) against the structural factors that made change inevitable (economic crisis, Angola failure, sanctions, internal unrest, ANC negotiating position under Mandela and Ramaphosa); reaches a supported judgement about 'how significant'. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of de Klerk's actions with limited analysis of wider factors. Emerging: Narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, the conference co-ordinated the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question' — the systematic murder of Europe's Jewish population — with participation from multiple Reich ministries). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the White Rose resistance movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. students at Munich University, among them Hans and Sophie Scholl, handed out leaflets attacking the regime and were executed on 22 February 1943). Secure: Names a valid feature with some detail. Developing: States a feature without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Stalingrad (1942–43) was a turning point in Germany's experience of the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses military significance (encirclement of 300,000+ German troops, surrender of ~91,000), impact on civilian morale (SD reports of defeatism), change in military fortunes (Germany retreating from 1943), political impact (Hitler's authority questioned by elites). Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why opposition to the Nazi regime developed during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed forms of resistance with precise evidence (e.g. White Rose — students, leaflets, executed February 1943 after Stalingrad; July Plot — von Stauffenberg's bomb attack 20 July 1944, failed, mass purge followed). Analysis explains why wartime resistance developed. Secure: Two forms with relevant evidence. Developing: Two forms with limited analysis. Emerging: One form or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the impact of Allied bombing on the German war effort and civilian morale in the years 1942–1945?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs the impact of bombing (Dresden, industrial targets, civilian casualties, SD morale reports) against other factors affecting the war effort (Eastern Front defeats, food and labour shortages, growing resistance). Uses Dresden figures precisely (22,700–25,000 — 2010 historical commission). Secure: Considers bombing's impact and compares with other factors with evidence. Developing: Describes bombing without comparative analysis. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that the Holocaust was the result of a long-term Nazi plan rather than wartime circumstances and escalation. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Engages with intentionalist vs functionalist historiographical debate without naming it as such: considers evidence of long-term intent (Mein Kampf, Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht) against evidence of wartime escalation (Einsatzgruppen 1941, Wannsee 1942 coordination, role of conquest of Soviet Union). Treats Holocaust with documentary specificity — six million figure, named methods, named events. Precise evidence; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both positions addressed with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Identifies a specific feature with accurate detail, e.g. the book argued that educated middle-class women were trapped by an unspoken cultural expectation that their only fulfilment lay in marriage and housekeeping, which Friedan called 'the problem that has no name.' Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to a book about women. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the feminist movement on legislation in the years 1963 to 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) the Equal Pay Act 1963 required equal pay for equal work, the first federal law against sex-based wage discrimination; (2) Title VII of the Civil Rights Act 1964 banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Equal Rights Amendment failed to be ratified despite passing Congress in 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign organised effective grassroots opposition; she argued the ERA would harm women (remove military draft exemption, end protective legislation); many states were conservative; the ERA's ratification window expired in 1982. Shows how these factors combined. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes the failure without explaining causes. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Stonewall riots of 1969 were significant for the development of LGBT rights in the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) the riots marked the first time LGBT people collectively fought back against routine police harassment, shifting from passive endurance to assertive protest; (2) within a year, LGBT organisations had formed across the country and the first Gay Pride marches were held, creating an organised movement that previously had not existed. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was NOW in advancing women's rights in the USA between 1966 and 1974?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis — NOW was significant because it combined lobbying, litigation and public campaigns; filed EEOC complaints; pushed Title VII enforcement; campaigned for ERA. But places it in context: Equal Pay Act and Title VII predated NOW; Friedan's book and the Commission had laid the groundwork; ERA failed; Roe v Wade came through Supreme Court rather than NOW campaigns. Compares NOW's significance to other factors. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes NOW without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the development and impact of feminist movements in the USA in the years 1963 to 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering The Feminine Mystique (1963), the Equal Pay Act (1963), Title VII (1964), founding of NOW (1966), ERA (1972 and ratification failure), Roe v Wade (1973), Stonewall (1969). Reaches an integrated judgement about what changed and what remained limited. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several developments with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the experience of Caribbean migrants in Britain in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Caribbean migrants faced widespread housing discrimination (1); 'No Coloured' signs in lodging houses were common in London and Birmingham, and the Race Relations Act did not prohibit this until 1965 (1). Feature 2: Caribbean migrants contributed to essential public services (1); the NHS actively recruited nurses from Barbados and Jamaica, and London Transport recruited in Barbados from 1956 (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962 was passed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons fully developed. Reason 1: The 1958 Notting Hill and Nottingham riots generated political pressure to restrict migration, with some politicians (wrongly) arguing that limiting arrivals would reduce racial tension. Reason 2: Growing public anxiety about housing pressure and employment competition in cities with large migrant communities provided political justification for introducing the voucher system, reversing the open-door policy of the 1948 Act. Secure: Both reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason explained. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Enoch Powell's 'Rivers of Blood' speech (1968) was historically significant.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the content (predicted catastrophic racial conflict from continued migration), the immediate political reaction (Powell sacked by Heath the next day, condemned by mainstream politicians), public opinion (polls showed substantial support), and long-term significance (accelerated shift to restriction, shaped decades of political debate on race). Notes that the speech was politically inflammatory rather than policy — it did not directly create legislation. Secure: Explains significance with at least two specific aspects. Developing: Describes the speech with some awareness of impact. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which Caribbean migrants contributed to British cultural and community life after 1948.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: Claudia Jones founded what became the Notting Hill Carnival in 1959, creating a major cultural institution in direct response to the 1958 riots (1-2 marks); Jones also founded the West Indian Gazette, Britain's first major Black newspaper (1 mark); Caribbean churches and community organisations maintained cultural identity and provided mutual support (1 mark). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the British government's response to Commonwealth migration was primarily hostile? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument noting the tension within government policy — the 1948 Act opened the door (welcoming); the NHS and employers actively recruited Caribbean workers; race relations legislation (1965, 1968, 1976) was genuinely progressive — but the 1962 and 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Acts and the 1971 Immigration Act progressively closed the door; argues that policy was contradictory rather than uniformly hostile. References Roy Jenkins's integration model and Enoch Powell's position as two ends of the spectrum. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides. Developing: Some comparison. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the 1971 Immigration Act and related legislation changed the lives of Commonwealth citizens already living in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two consequences with causal analysis. Consequence 1: The patriality requirement (grandparent born in Britain) effectively stripped British passport-holders like Kenyan Asians of meaningful citizenship rights, creating a category of de facto stateless people. Consequence 2: The Windrush generation's legal status became precarious — the destruction of landing cards by the Home Office decades later created the 'Windrush scandal' where long-settled residents could not prove their right to be in Britain. Secure: Two consequences with evidence. Developing: One explained. Emerging: General statements.

practice_questions.text: Outline two consequences of the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961 for Cold War relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed consequences, each with specific supporting detail (e.g. refugee exodus halted; Kennedy's visit reinforced Western commitment). Secure: Two identified consequences with some development. Developing: Two consequences identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.
