practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the USSR established the Warsaw Pact in 1955.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons with specific evidence (West Germany's NATO entry; desire to formalise Soviet military control of Eastern Europe). Secure: Two reasons developed with supporting detail. Developing: Two reasons identified but development is limited. Emerging: One basic reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Hungarian Uprising of 1956 was significant for Cold War relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument linking specific evidence (Nagy's withdrawal from Warsaw Pact; Soviet tank invasion; Western non-intervention) to a clear judgement about Cold War rules of the game. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Descriptive points.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Warsaw Pact signed in 1955.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific supporting detail (e.g. Soviet commanders held top posts; created five days after West Germany joined NATO). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features identified without detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Berlin Wall was built in August 1961.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes (refugee exodus draining the GDR; Khrushchev's Vienna Summit ultimatum rejected by Kennedy) with causal analysis and specific detail. Secure: Two causes developed with relevant evidence. Developing: One cause well-developed or two causes briefly stated. Emerging: Simple descriptive statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Hungarian Uprising of 1956 established the rules of Cold War conflict in Europe.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of multiple causal factors (Soviet military response; Western inaction; Warsaw Pact framework) linked coherently to the question. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Defence of the Realm Act (DORA) 1914.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific power (e.g. the government could requisition factories for war production) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. this meant private businesses could be compelled to switch from commercial goods to armaments without their owners' consent — a direct extension of state power into private enterprise). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to government having more power. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Beveridge Report (1942).
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. it identified five 'Giant Evils' — Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness — as the specific problems a welfare state needed to defeat; it proposed comprehensive national insurance covering all citizens 'from the cradle to the grave' — funded by contributions from workers, employers and the state). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the First World War led to a significant expansion of state power in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (the scale of the military effort required industrial coordination that the private sector alone could not deliver — DORA allowed requisitioning of factories, food control and press censorship; the war required mass mobilisation of civilian workers, including women, blurring the line between civil and military life; total war revealed the state's capacity to direct the economy, setting a precedent; the experience of wartime state action made post-war social reform politically imaginable). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes DORA without explaining why war expanded the state.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Attlee government's welfare reforms were a cross-party achievement rather than solely a Labour one.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (the Beveridge Report 1942 was by a Liberal economist — Attlee implemented a Liberal plan; the 1944 Education Act was passed by the wartime coalition under Conservative Butler; Churchill's wartime coalition had commissioned the Beveridge Report and built the administrative groundwork; the Conservatives under Churchill in 1951 kept the NHS and most nationalised industries, demonstrating cross-party acceptance). Considers why it matters historically that the welfare state was not a purely Labour project. Secure: two factors with relevant evidence. Developing: describes Attlee's reforms without explaining the cross-party context. Emerging: describes the NHS as a Labour achievement without engaging with the question.

practice_questions.text: How significant were the two world wars in changing the role of the state in Britain between 1914 and 1979? [You may consider: DORA; the Beveridge Report; the welfare state; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing the scale of change (DORA and wartime powers vastly extended state reach; Beveridge and Attlee created permanent welfare institutions; nationalisation created a mixed economy; NHS became central to British life) and continuity/limits (post-war consensus frayed in the 1970s; EEC entry raised sovereignty questions; Winter of Discontent showed limits of state-managed economy; Thatcher's election in 1979 signalled a coming challenge to the consensus). Overall judgement on significance. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes welfare state creation accurately but does not address the question of significance or longer-term limits. Emerging: narrative without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the key steps in building the post-war welfare state between 1942 and 1951.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points in sequence (Beveridge Report 1942 — identified Five Giants, proposed welfare state; 1944 Education Act — secondary education for all; Labour landslide 1945; National Insurance Act 1946 — welfare safety net; NHS founded 5 July 1948 — free healthcare; nationalisation of coal, railways, electricity, steel 1946-51). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to the NHS being founded.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Household Responsibility System.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. leasing arrangements, surplus-selling rights, replacement of commune system). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without clear detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Special Economic Zones established in 1980.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise detail (e.g. locations, types of investment permitted, different rules from rest of China, purpose). Secure: Two features, each with some detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Deng Xiaoping introduced the Household Responsibility System.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (failure of commune system, need to increase agricultural output after famine, political desire to break with Maoist collectivisation). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Four Modernisations for China's development after 1978.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis across criteria (immediate policy change, longer-term economic development, winners and losers, contrast with Maoist era); counter-argument considered. Secure: Clear argument about significance with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis. Emerging: Describes policies with minimal argument about significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did Deng's economic reforms represent a break from Mao's economic policies? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence of change (market mechanisms, SEZs, HRS, opening to foreign investment) against continuity (one-party control, state sector maintained, Chen Yun's birdcage model, official '70-30' Mao verdict); specific evidence; balanced conclusion. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides; some weighing. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why China established full diplomatic relations with the United States in 1979.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (access to capital and technology, strategic counterweight to Soviet Union, continuation of Nixon-era rapprochement). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two criticisms of the New Deal from left-wing politicians or movements.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct criticism, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: Huey Long’s Share Our Wealth movement wanted large fortunes capped and every family guaranteed a minimum income; Francis Townsend wanted a $200 monthly pension for everyone over 60; Father Coughlin attacked the New Deal as a tool of big business and bankers.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the New Deal failed to help African Americans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both ways fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the Social Security Act excluded domestic servants and agricultural labourers — the jobs held by most Black Americans in the South — meaning the first federal safety net was racially discriminatory in practice; the AAA’s production reduction payments went to landowners, causing landlords to evict sharecroppers who were disproportionately Black). Secure: Both ways explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Supreme Court was a significant opponent of the New Deal.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the constitutional basis for the court’s opposition (separation of powers, property rights, limits on federal power); the specific strikes (NRA 1935, AAA 1936); the political consequences (court-packing plan proposed and failed in 1937); and the longer-term significance (court effectively backed down — ‘switch in time that saved nine’ — but damaged Roosevelt’s standing). Secure: Two or more aspects explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One aspect explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific cases.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Huey Long's 'Share Our Wealth' programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: it proposed capping personal fortunes at $50 million; it promised every American family a minimum annual income of $2,000; its clubs claimed over 7 million members by 1935.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that opposition to the New Deal showed it was failing the American people? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that uses opposition as evidence of failure in some respects (AAA excluded sharecroppers, SSA excluded Black workers, NRA struck down) while arguing that the scale and diversity of opposition also reflects the New Deal’s significance (both right and left objected, for opposing reasons); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence across multiple dimensions of opposition and its meaning. Developing: Some awareness of different types of opposition. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are given in this section.

practice_questions.text: Sources A and B give different views of the New Deal's impact on African Americans. Source A says it made meaningful progress by involving Black Americans in federal programmes for the first time. Source B says it reinforced and institutionalised racial inequality through discriminatory policy design. How far do the two sources agree? Use both sources and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (progress vs. reinforcement of inequality, individual vs. structural focus); tests both against own knowledge (Eleanor Roosevelt, Black Cabinet, WPA employment for A; SSA exclusions, AAA displacement, FHA redlining for B); explains why the two views differ (focus on rhetoric vs. practice, evidence selected, political perspective). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Declaration of Breda reassured the political nation in 1660.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. it promised a general pardon except for those Parliament chose to exclude, and it left that decision, religion, army pay and land disputes to Parliament rather than to the King alone. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why George Monck was so important to the Restoration of 1660.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons, e.g. he marched south from Scotland in January 1660 with a disciplined army and steadied a chaotic situation, then readmitted the MPs excluded in 1648 so the Long Parliament could dissolve itself and call elections. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the republic collapsed between 1658 and 1660.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple causes (Oliver Cromwell's death removed only unifying figure, Richard's lack of authority, army factionalism, constitutional instability of 1659, public exhaustion with military rule) linked together. Secure: Two causes developed. Developing: One cause. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: The Declaration of Breda was the most important reason for the Restoration in 1660. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs Declaration of Breda (reassuring content, deferred to Parliament) against Monck's military role (provided the mechanism), Richard Cromwell's failure (removed alternative), and general exhaustion with military rule (created the need). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Considers multiple factors. Developing: Mainly focuses on one factor. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Richard Cromwell was unable to maintain power as Lord Protector in 1658–1659.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (no military reputation, army hostility, Parliament's challenge to army role, lack of father's personal authority, inability to manage army-Parliament tensions). Linked argument. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles II's restoration in 1660 did not simply reverse all the changes made since 1642.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that prerogative courts were not restored, Triennial Act remained, Parliament retained rights confirmed 1641; Restoration was a negotiated settlement, not unconditional return; Indemnity Act acknowledged the past had to be buried not reversed. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the site chosen for Kenilworth Castle suited its builders.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. the sandstone ridge gave a dry, raised platform above the valley floor; the brooks running through that valley could be dammed, which is what King John did to make the Great Mere. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Kenilworth Castle's buildings changed between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. John of Gaunt wanted a residence fit for the richest magnate in England, so he built a great hall with wide windows; Robert Dudley needed rooms fit for a queen, so Leicester's Building put comfort and glass ahead of defence. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the location of Kenilworth Castle was important for its function.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons that tie the site to what the castle had to do, e.g. the sandstone ridge gave a defensible platform above the valley; the Great Mere flooded the ground to the south and west, so attackers could only approach from the north and east. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: a simple statement about location.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the physical fabric of Kenilworth Castle reflects the changing priorities of its owners over time.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons with named fabric, e.g. Caesar's Tower has walls about 5 metres thick and few openings, built to survive a siege; Leicester's Building has large glazed windows and comfortable lodgings, built for display. Secure: two phases with relevant detail. Developing: one phase developed. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Compare what John of Gaunt's great hall and Caesar's Tower suggest about why Kenilworth Castle was built and used. Explain why they give different impressions.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: says what each building shows (thick walls, few openings and a defensible stair in the tower; a wide hall with large windows and a timber roof), explains the difference from their dates and purposes (a Norman lord's stronghold of the 1120s; a great magnate's palace of the 1370s), and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: both compared with some explanation. Developing: some comparison. Emerging: describes each separately.

practice_questions.text: Compare what Dugdale's 1656 engravings of Kenilworth and the ruins standing today suggest about the damage done by the slighting. Explain why they differ.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: says what each shows (Dugdale records the ruins within a few years of the slighting, with the mere already drained; the site today has lost more stone to later robbing and clearance), explains the difference by date, by later use of the site and by Dugdale's royalist sympathies, and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: both compared with some explanation. Developing: some comparison. Emerging: describes each separately.

practice_questions.text: Explain what the Georgian terraces on Fournier Street show about the Huguenot community.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. substantial brick houses with wide upper windows for looms show weaving wealth; their quality contrasts sharply with the far poorer courts nearby). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Christ Church Spitalfields is useful evidence for the history of the area.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. Parliament funded it under the 1711 act for fifty new churches, which shows Anglican concern about a district of foreign Protestants; its parish registers from 1729 record names and origins). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Brick Lane Jamme Masjid building provides evidence for successive waves of migration in Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed explanation naming all four uses (Huguenot chapel 1743, Methodist chapel, synagogue c.1897, mosque 1976) with specific dates and contextual explanation of what each transition reveals about migration history. Secure: Three uses identified with some contextual explanation. Developing: Two uses with basic explanation. Emerging: Only one use or vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Huguenot weavers chose to settle in Spitalfields specifically rather than in the City of London.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation covering lower rents, exclusion from City guilds, semi-rural space for workshops, proximity to London markets, and the attraction of an existing refugee community, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one factor explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Study Sources A and B about migration to Spitalfields [supplied in the exam]. Compare what the two sources show about how migrants were received in the area.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained comparison using precise detail from both sources, supported by Spitalfields knowledge, judging what each source shows and what it leaves out. Secure: Clear comparison with some contextual knowledge. Developing: Sources treated separately; comparison limited. Emerging: Describes one source, or describes both without comparing.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the layout and buildings of Spitalfields suited newly arrived migrants.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. it lay outside the City walls, so rents were low and guild rules did not apply; semi-rural plots left room for weaving workshops close to London markets). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the One Child Policy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. when it was introduced, how it was enforced, who designed it). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without clear detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of educational change under Deng Xiaoping.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise detail (e.g. gaokao restored 1977, six million candidates, compulsory primary education extended). Secure: Two features, each with some detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the One Child Policy led to human rights concerns.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (coercive local enforcement including forced abortion/sterilisation, sex-selective abortion, female infanticide, state intervention in bodily autonomy). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the restoration of the gaokao in 1977 for Chinese society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis across criteria (immediate access to education for Cultural Revolution generation, longer-term meritocracy signal, urban-rural inequalities, political symbolism of break from Maoism); counter-argument considered. Secure: Clear argument with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis. Emerging: Describes the gaokao with minimal argument about significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did Deng's social policies improve the lives of women in China? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence of improvement (1980 Marriage Law, formal employment equality, Women's Federation) against continued disadvantage (redundancy targeting, One Child Policy intensifying son-preference, hukou limits); specific evidence; balanced conclusion. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides; some weighing. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the One Child Policy was introduced in 1979.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (Song Jian's demographic modelling, fear that population growth would undermine economic modernisation, specific concern about resource pressure). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the US federal government expanded its powers during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct way, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: conscription through Selective Service, which drafted around 10 million Americans; the War Production Board directed industrial output; the government controlled wages, prices and rationing.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Japanese-American internment during the Second World War is considered a violation of civil liberties.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. around two-thirds of those interned were US citizens born in the United States — EO 9066 effectively punished people for their ethnic background rather than any proven disloyalty; the Supreme Court in Korematsu v United States upheld the internment in 1944 on grounds of military necessity, demonstrating that even constitutional protections could be suspended during wartime, a precedent considered deeply troubling by later jurists). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Executive Order 8802 was significant for the history of civil rights in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance in multiple dimensions — it was the first presidential civil rights executive order since Reconstruction; it was won through the threat of mass protest (A. Philip Randolph’s threatened March on Washington), establishing political pressure as a civil rights strategy; it created the FEPC; but also explains limits (FEPC underfunded, no enforcement, military remained segregated). Secure: Two or more dimensions explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One dimension explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Detroit Race Riot of 1943.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct feature, maximum 2 marks. Supporting detail is not needed for this question. Examples: 34 people were killed over three days in June 1943; 25 of the dead were African American; federal troops were needed to restore order; wartime migration had put severe pressure on housing and jobs.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Second World War was the foundation of the civil rights movement in the United States? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges wartime foundations (EO 8802, Tuskegee Airmen, Double V campaign, Randolph’s March on Washington threat, contradictions of segregated military) while also recognising earlier roots (NAACP since 1909, Red Summer 1919, Garvey movement) and post-war continuity (Truman’s EO 9981); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both wartime and longer-term context. Developing: Some awareness of continuity and change. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. No marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar are given in this section.

practice_questions.text: Sources A and B give different views of women's wartime roles. Source A says the war permanently transformed women's status in American society. Source B says the changes were temporary and women were pushed back into domestic roles after 1945. How far do the two sources agree? Use both sources and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (permanence vs. temporariness of change, propaganda vs. reality); tests both against own knowledge (19 million women employed 1944, Rosie the Riveter imagery for A; post-war pressure to return home, lower pay than male counterparts, 1950s domestic ideology for B); explains why the two views differ (contemporary vs. retrospective evidence, feminist vs. traditional perspective). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Describe two pressures that led to the Military Service Act (1916).
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. voluntary recruitment could not replace losses at battles like the Somme — on 1 July 1916 alone there were 57,470 British casualties — so conscription was needed to maintain the Army's strength). Developing: vague (e.g. 'there weren't enough soldiers').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the Blitz on the British civilian population.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. German bombers targeted British cities on 57 consecutive nights from September 1940, killing approximately 43,000 civilians; about 1.5 million people, including 827,000 schoolchildren, were evacuated from the cities to protect them from bombing. Developing: identifies impacts without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Representation of the People Act (1918) was a consequence of the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — connects women's wartime labour in munitions and other roles, men's mass military service, the political argument that those who served could not be denied the vote, and Lloyd George's recognition that wartime mobilisation required political recognition. Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why total war increased the power of the British state over everyday life.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers DORA (censorship, pub hours, rationing), Emergency Powers Act (1940), conscription of men and women, food rationing, evacuation, and why the military pressures made these interventions necessary. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the two world wars transform the relationship between the British state and its citizens? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers political change (franchise 1918/1928), economic change (income tax, rationing, state direction of industry), social change (women's roles, class mixing in service), the post-war welfare state as lasting legacy, and elements of continuity (class structure survived, voluntary tradition persisted in some areas); reaches a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument covering transformation and continuity. Developing: Mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Beveridge Report (1942) was significant for the future of Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains its content (five giants, universal welfare), immediate reception (630,000 copies, wartime discussion), political consequences (1945 Labour landslide), and the post-war welfare state it inspired (NHS 1948, national insurance). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Nuremberg Trials (1945–1946).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the International Military Tribunal charged twenty-four leading Nazis and tried twenty-two before judges from the four Allied powers on charges including crimes against humanity, with twelve receiving death sentences). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the de-Nazification process in the Western occupation zones.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the Fragebogen questionnaire of 131 questions was completed by millions of Germans and sorted them into five categories). Secure: Names a valid feature with some detail. Developing: States a feature without specific detail. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the de-Nazification process in the Western zones was only partially effective.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses multiple reasons — millions of Fragebogen underreported Nazi involvement; tribunals overwhelmed by volume; witnesses died; Cold War making German reintegration more important than thorough prosecution; many genuine offenders received light sentences. Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the experiences of people in East and West Germany differed in the years 1949–1955.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed differences with precise evidence (e.g. FRG Wirtschaftswunder created rapid economic growth and rising living standards vs GDR's quotas and poor conditions; FRG democratic elections vs GDR one-party SED rule; June 1953 uprising crushed by Soviet tanks in East vs democratic stability in West). Secure: Two differences with relevant evidence. Developing: Two differences with limited analysis. Emerging: One difference or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant were the Nuremberg Trials in addressing the crimes of the Nazi regime?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs Nuremberg's genuine achievements (new international law, 'following orders' principle rejected, senior Nazis convicted) against limitations (only 24 defendants at the main trial, victor's justice criticism, many perpetrators tried only at later trials or not at all, de-Nazification wound down by 1951). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Considers achievements and limitations with evidence. Developing: Describes Nuremberg without evaluating limitations. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that the division of Germany into East and West by 1955 was the inevitable result of the Allied occupation after 1945. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument considering factors that made division likely (different Allied political systems, Soviet land reform and communist GDR, Deutschmark introduction, Berlin Blockade hardening attitudes) against factors that might have produced a different outcome (original intent for a united Germany, Yalta and Potsdam agreements for joint administration). Uses precise dates and events throughout. Secure: Both positions addressed with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Macpherson Report's findings about the Metropolitan Police.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The report found the Metropolitan Police to be 'institutionally racist' (1); this was the first time a government inquiry had applied this diagnosis to a British institution, making it historically significant (1). Feature 2: The report made 70 recommendations for reform (1); it led to significant changes in police conduct, race relations law and the training of officers (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why asylum seekers became a major political issue in Britain in the 1990s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons developed with evidence. Reason 1: Global conflicts (Bosnia, Kosovo, Iraq, Afghanistan) drove large numbers of people to seek refuge in Western Europe; the number of applications to Britain rose sharply, creating public and political anxiety about scale. Reason 2: Media coverage using language of 'floods' and 'waves' inflamed public opinion; newspapers often failed to distinguish between asylum seekers (with legal rights under the 1951 Refugee Convention) and economic migrants, creating confusion and hostility. Secure: Both with evidence. Developing: One explained. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why EU enlargement in 2004 had significant consequences for Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that Britain did not impose transitional restrictions on A8 workers (unlike France and Germany); the resulting rapid migration from Poland and other A8 countries filled economic gaps but also strained local services; political controversy grew over housing, schools and health; the experience directly fed into the 2016 Brexit referendum debate about EU free movement. Secure: Explains at least two consequences with evidence. Developing: Notes some consequences. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two arguments made in the Parekh Report (2000) about British identity.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: the report argued Britain should embrace its identity as a 'community of communities' (1), meaning different groups maintain distinct identities while sharing civic values (1); it recommended that 'Britishness' be redefined as a civic rather than ethnic identity (1), open to all who shared democratic values regardless of ethnic origin (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that immigration remained the most divisive issue in British politics between 1981 and 2010? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument considering immigration alongside other divisive issues (Miners' Strike 1984-85, Thatcherism, devolution) and assessing relative significance; considers how immigration's political salience shifted from asylum (1990s) to EU migration (2004-10); uses specific evidence from the Parekh Report, Macpherson Report and Brexit debate context; acknowledges that while contentious, mainstream parties shared restrictive positions. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from multiple dimensions. Developing: Some comparison but mainly descriptive. Emerging: Lists events without argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the British Nationality Act of 1981 changed the legal position of Commonwealth citizens.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two changes with causal analysis. Change 1: Created multiple tiers of nationality — only 'British Citizens' with parent/grandparent born in UK retained right of abode, removing the broad citizenship of the 1948 Act. Change 2: Made patriality (ancestral connection to Britain) the basis of the right to settle, meaning Commonwealth citizens who had held legal rights since 1948 now found those rights removed — this directly contributed to the Windrush scandal decades later. Secure: Two changes explained. Developing: One change explained. Emerging: General statements.

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why Khrushchev placed Soviet missiles in Cuba in 1962.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed reasons, each with specific supporting detail (e.g. to deter US invasion after Bay of Pigs; to close the missile gap with the USA). Secure: Two identified reasons with some development. Developing: Two reasons identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis for superpower relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed consequences with specific evidence (hotline established 1963; Partial Test Ban Treaty; both sides chastened by how close conflict came). Secure: Two consequences with supporting detail. Developing: Two consequences identified but development is limited. Emerging: One basic consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Cuban Missile Crisis was the most dangerous moment of the Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument with specific evidence (Black Saturday; submarine near-launch; 13-day timeline) linked to a clear judgement. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Some explanation with limited detail. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of Kennedy's response to the discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific detail (e.g. naval quarantine announced 22 October; ExComm formed to consider options). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the secret Jupiter missile deal is significant for historians studying the Cuban Missile Crisis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Well-developed explanation linking the secret deal to the resolution of the crisis and to the post-Cold War opening of archives that changed historical understanding. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Brief descriptive statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why 27 October 1962 (Black Saturday) was the most critical day of the Cuban Missile Crisis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of multiple causal factors (U-2 shot down; submarine depth-charge incident; Vasili Arkhipov intervention) with clear links to how close nuclear war came. Secure: Clear explanation with evidence. Developing: Some explanation but development limited. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Johnson's Great Society programme.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names a specific programme with accurate detail, e.g. Medicare, introduced in 1965, provided federal health insurance for Americans aged 65 and over, addressing the problem that many elderly people could not afford medical care. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to welfare reforms. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the anti-Vietnam War protest movement in the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks in total, one for each correct feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) the Moratorium of October 1969 brought an estimated two million Americans into the streets in the largest anti-war demonstration in US history to that point; (2) after the Kent State shootings in May 1970, 450 universities went on strike and the movement radicalised further. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Tet Offensive of 1968 was such a significant turning point in the Vietnam War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple effects with specific evidence — the scale of the offensive (attacks on 100+ South Vietnamese cities and towns, including the US Embassy) destroyed the credibility of official claims that the war was being won; Cronkite's 'stalemate' editorial was a landmark moment; Johnson's approval ratings collapsed and he withdrew from the presidential race in March 1968. Shows the chain of consequences. Secure: Two or more effects with evidence. Developing: Describes the offensive without explaining its impact. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Nixon's domestic policies were more complex than simply 'conservative.'
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) Nixon proposed the Family Assistance Plan, a guaranteed minimum income for poor families that was in some ways more radical than Johnson's welfare programmes — it failed because it faced opposition from both left and right; (2) Nixon created the Environmental Protection Agency (1970) and Title IX (1972), which banned sex discrimination in federally funded education, both significant progressive reforms. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Watergate scandal in changing American political life?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis covering significance — first presidential resignation in US history; deepened distrust of government already damaged by Vietnam; exposed abuse of executive power (CIA, FBI misuse, hush money, enemies' lists); led to Congressional reforms limiting presidential power. But places it in context: distrust had been building since Vietnam; the institutions worked — the courts, Senate investigation and press all functioned as checks; Ford's pardon limited accountability. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Watergate without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the political, economic and social divisions in the USA in the years 1964 to 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay showing how Vietnam, the Great Society, Nixon's America and Watergate connected as causes and expressions of division — the war divided the Democrats, undermined Great Society funding, produced the anti-war movement, Chicago 1968, Kent State 1970, the Moratorium; Nixon exploited divisions to win power but Watergate ended his presidency in disgrace. Reaches an integrated judgement about the nature of American divisions in this period. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several causes of division with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events in sequence with limited analysis. Emerging: Brief narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Jewish settlement after the 1880s changed Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed changes with precise evidence (e.g. around 120,000 Jewish migrants reached Britain between 1880 and 1914 and many worked in the garment trade; Yiddish became a street language and the Brick Lane chapel became a synagogue around 1897). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one change. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Study Sources A and B about the Battle of Cable Street [supplied in the exam]. Compare what the two sources show about the events of 4 October 1936.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained comparison using precise detail from both sources, supported by Spitalfields knowledge, judging what each source shows and what it leaves out. Secure: Clear comparison with some contextual knowledge. Developing: Sources treated separately; comparison limited. Emerging: Describes one source, or describes both without comparing.

practice_questions.text: Using your knowledge of Spitalfields, explain how the physical fabric of the area provides evidence for successive waves of migration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed explanation naming specific buildings (Brick Lane Jamme Masjid, Christ Church, Fournier Street terraces) and linking them to specific communities, showing how physical changes reveal migration history. Secure: Two or three specific examples with explanation. Developing: General reference to buildings without specific details. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why successive migrant communities in Spitalfields faced hostile reception from the settled population.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation covering economic competition (Irish dock labourers vs. English workers; garment trade), religious and racial prejudice (anti-Catholic, anti-semitism, racism against Bangladeshis), legal measures (Aliens Act 1905), and the specific experience of each community, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least two communities' experiences covered. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Cable Street (1936) is remembered as important in the East End.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with precise evidence (e.g. around 100,000 Jewish, Irish and trade union demonstrators blocked Mosley's route and the march was turned back; the day became a lasting symbol of local solidarity against fascism). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one reason. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Bangladeshi settlement changed Spitalfields from the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed changes with precise evidence (e.g. work in the garment trade echoed the Huguenot weavers, and Brick Lane restaurants gave the area the name Banglatown; the synagogue became the Jamme Masjid in 1976). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one change. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Government of National Unity formed after the 1994 election.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the GNU AND gives a precise feature, e.g. any party with at least 5 per cent of the vote received cabinet seats; or F.W. de Klerk became one of two Deputy Presidents. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to a coalition government. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of South Africa's first non-racial election of April 1994.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the 1994 election AND gives a precise feature, e.g. about 19.7 million people voted over 27–29 April, or seats were shared out in proportion to each party's share of the vote. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to a free election. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the 1994 election result was considered significant both inside and outside South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) it was the first non-racial election, giving millions of black South Africans a vote for the first time — itself a historic achievement; (2) it produced a large ANC majority that gave Mandela a democratic mandate to lead reconstruction; (3) the international community (UN, Commonwealth observers) validated the process as free and fair. Each reason with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two limitations of the changes brought about by the 1994 election in South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the sunset clauses left apartheid-era civil servants and security officials in post, preventing restructuring of the state; (2) no significant land redistribution occurred, leaving South Africa one of the most unequal societies on earth. Secure: Two reasons with good detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the election of April 1994 mattered so much to millions of South Africans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with precise evidence, e.g. black South Africans had been shut out of national elections throughout apartheid, so casting a vote was itself the end of that exclusion; the result put Nelson Mandela in office after 27 years in prison, which made the change feel complete. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of the election.

practice_questions.text: How far did the end of apartheid in 1994 represent a complete transformation of South African society? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing what changed (formal apartheid ended, non-racial democracy established, Mandela as president, TRC process) against what remained the same (land distribution, economic inequality, sunset clauses preserving state structures); reaches a supported judgement on 'how far'. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of 1994 with limited analysis of structural continuities. Emerging: Narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Miners' Strike of 1984-85.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. the strike was called by Arthur Scargill's NUM without a national ballot) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. this weakened the union's position because it allowed the government and media to question its democratic legitimacy, making it harder for other unions and public opinion to back the strikers). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to a miners' dispute. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways CND challenged government policy in the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. CND organised mass demonstrations attracting over 100,000 members when NATO stationed Cruise missiles in Western Europe — this created sustained political pressure on both parties; the Greenham Common Women's Peace Camp maintained a continuous presence outside the USAF base in Berkshire from 1981, generating international media coverage and keeping nuclear policy visible in public debate). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: vague reference to people protesting against nuclear weapons.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Miners' Strike of 1984-85 ended in defeat for the NUM.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (Thatcher's government had prepared for the confrontation — coal stocks were stockpiled and alternative fuels arranged, so the economic pressure of the strike was reduced; the NUM did not hold a national ballot before calling the strike, weakening its democratic legitimacy and preventing the TUC from calling general union support; violent confrontations such as Orgreave alienated public opinion; community division and family hardship among mining communities eventually broke solidarity). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes the strike without explaining why it failed.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Greenpeace was effective in challenging government and corporate decisions despite not holding political power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (direct action tactics — occupying the Brent Spar platform and sailing ships into nuclear test zones — generated media coverage that made ignoring the issue politically costly; consumer pressure during the Brent Spar dispute led to a European boycott of Shell that changed the company's decision despite government support for deep-sea disposal; Greenpeace demonstrated that environmental concerns had broad public support, creating electoral incentives for government to act; high-profile campaigns shaped the political agenda on nuclear testing, whaling and eventually climate change). Secure: two factors with relevant evidence. Developing: describes Greenpeace campaigns accurately but does not explain the mechanism by which they were effective. Emerging: vague reference to public support.

practice_questions.text: How far did pressure groups in the period 1958-2007 successfully challenge the power of Parliament and government? [You may consider: CND; Greenpeace; the Miners' Strike; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both success and failure — success: Greenpeace Brent Spar victory; CND influenced Labour policy; mass protests (Iraq 2003 march) kept issues in public debate; failure: CND did not achieve nuclear disarmament; Miners' Strike ended in defeat; Blair ignored the 2003 Iraq march; Parliament and government retained ultimate decision-making power. Overall judgement about the extent of pressure group success and what kinds of pressure groups were more/less effective. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence from named groups; some imbalance. Developing: describes pressure group activities accurately but does not weigh success against failure. Emerging: narrative of events without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main features of Prime Ministerial power under Thatcher or Blair.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points about either Thatcher or Blair (or both with comparison) — Thatcher: centralised decision-making; sidelined dissenting cabinet ministers; confrontational approach to unions; removed by own MPs 1990 over poll tax and Europe; Blair: 179-seat majority 1997; 'sofa government' style; Iraq War 2003 against cabinet advice and mass public opposition; constitutional reforms — devolution, Human Rights Act. Secure: two or three relevant points with supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to these PMs having a lot of power.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Kenilworth Castle was valuable to whoever held it in the thirteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. it stood in the middle of England, so a garrison there could reach trouble in any direction; the Great Mere and the great tower made it almost impossible to storm, as the 1266 siege showed. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Kenilworth Castle needed a large household under John of Gaunt.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. Gaunt ran his estates from Kenilworth, so clerks and stewards were needed to keep the accounts and hear tenants; entertaining important guests demanded cooks, servants and steady supplies of fish, grain and wine. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Siege of Kenilworth 1266 lasted so long.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons tied to the castle itself, e.g. the Great Mere kept siege engines and miners away from most of the walls; the great tower and stocked stores let the garrison hold out until disease and hunger, not assault, forced terms. Secure: two features linked to the length of the siege. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Kenilworth Castle's function changed between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons with evidence for each phase, e.g. in 1266 it was a fortress that a royal army could not storm; by the 1570s Leicester's Building and the 1575 entertainment made it a stage for courtly display. Secure: two phases with relevant detail. Developing: one phase developed. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Compare what Leicester's Building and the printed account of the 1575 entertainment suggest about why Robert Dudley spent so much on Kenilworth. Explain why they agree or differ.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: says what each shows (a range of comfortable lodgings with large windows built for one guest; nineteen days of pageants, fireworks, hunting and banquets), explains that both were arguments about Dudley's fitness to marry the queen, and notes that a printed account was meant to be read and admired. Secure: both compared with some explanation. Developing: some comparison. Emerging: describes each separately.

practice_questions.text: Compare what John of Gaunt's household accounts and the castle's surviving kitchen range suggest about how Kenilworth Castle was run. Explain what each can and cannot tell you.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: says what each shows (accounts name the goods bought and the wages paid; the kitchen range shows the scale of cooking and where the work was done), explains that accounts record money rather than daily life while the fabric shows space but names nobody, and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: both compared with some explanation. Developing: some comparison. Emerging: describes each separately.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the slighting of 1649–50 changed the appearance of Kenilworth Castle.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed points with precise site detail, e.g. the north wall of the Norman keep was demolished, which gives the great tower its cut-away look today, and the outer bailey wall and battlements were breached. Secure: one point explained with site detail. Developing: a point identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Kenilworth Castle was used during the Civil War (1642–1646).
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed points with precise site detail, e.g. Charles I used the castle before Edgehill, then Parliament garrisoned it from late 1642 and used it as a Midlands base; Royalist attempts to drive Parliament out of Warwickshire failed, so the castle never faced a long siege. Secure: one point explained with site detail. Developing: a point identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament ordered the slighting of Kenilworth Castle in 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Parliament's systematic slighting policy (too expensive to garrison, too dangerous to leave intact), connects to the political context of the Commonwealth's establishment in 1649, and identifies specific physical actions taken at Kenilworth (wall demolition, roof removal, mere drainage). Secure: Two or more reasons with some site-specific detail. Developing: One reason or general policy without Kenilworth detail. Emerging: Simple reference to Parliament slighting it.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the physical evidence at Kenilworth Castle today reflects the events of the Civil War period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Connects three or more visible features (demolished north wall, roofless great hall and residential ranges, absence of the mere) to documented slighting actions of 1649-50. Explains that these are products of deliberate Parliamentary policy, not decay or neglect. Secure: Two features connected to slighting. Developing: One feature connected. Emerging: Vague reference to the castle being ruined.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a visit to Kenilworth Castle for understanding the impact of the English Civil War on historic buildings?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates what the physical site reveals (visible slighting damage, scale of deliberate destruction, loss of the mere) and what it cannot show (motivations of Parliament, broader impact of the war on people, what the castle looked like before slighting). Considers the limitations of physical evidence without documentary context. Secure: Considers strengths and limitations with site-specific evidence. Developing: Mainly describes what can be seen. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: The slighting of Kenilworth Castle in 1649–50 tells us more about Parliament's attitude to potential Royalist threats than about the castle's military value. How far does the evidence support this view?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Uses evidence of the slighting (demolition, draining) alongside contextual knowledge of Parliament's wider slighting programme to evaluate whether Kenilworth was slighted for political reasons or genuine military threat assessment. Considers the castle's limited fighting role in the war. Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Uses evidence and context to make an argument. Developing: Describes the slighting without evaluating the statement. Emerging: Mostly describes.

practice_questions.text: Explain what Charles Booth's poverty maps reveal about Spitalfields, and what they do not.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. the colour-coded maps from 1889 show poverty street by street and place the poorest workers in courts off Brick Lane; Booth's categories carry his own Victorian assumptions about class). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why parish registers are useful but incomplete evidence for migration in Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. Christ Church registers from 1729 record baptisms, marriages and burials, and name spellings hint at national origins; they cover only those who used the Anglican church, so Jewish, Nonconformist and later Muslim residents are missing). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Using your knowledge of Spitalfields, explain how oral history provides evidence that written records cannot.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed explanation identifying specific oral history sources (BBC Jewish East End recordings, Tower Hamlets Bangladeshi community recordings) and explaining what they reveal (daily life, personal experience of prejudice, Yiddish culture) that parish registers and surveys do not capture, with reference to limitations of memory. Secure: Two or three specific examples with explanation. Developing: General reference to oral history without site-specific examples. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Using Sources A and B [supplied in exam] and your own knowledge, explain how useful these sources are for understanding migration in Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, integrated comparison that uses specific details from both sources, deploys Spitalfields-specific contextual knowledge (naming specific buildings, dates, communities), evaluates both the usefulness and limitations of each source, and reaches a judgement on their relative value for the specific question. Secure: Clear comparison with some contextual knowledge and evaluation. Developing: Sources treated separately; some evaluation. Emerging: Describes sources without comparison or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the physical fabric of Spitalfields is particularly valuable as historical evidence for migration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation using specific examples (Jamme Masjid building's four uses, Fournier Street terraces, Christ Church) to show how physical fabric reveals migration patterns, economic status and community succession that documents alone cannot show, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with at least two specific examples. Developing: Some explanation with basic or generic evidence. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Henry Mayhew's journalism is valuable evidence for life in the East End.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed points with precise evidence (e.g. his accounts from the 1840s to the 1860s give first-hand detail about Irish street sellers and casual labourers who left no other record; his middle-class outlook and journalistic purpose shape what he reports). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence for at least one point. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple or vague points with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways CND changed how British people responded to war policy.
practice_questions.marks: Four marks are available. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. CND represented a new form of mass popular opposition to state nuclear weapons policy, with tens of thousands marching annually from Aldermaston to London, showing that wartime public responses had shifted from support to challenge). Developing: vague (e.g. 'people didn't want nuclear weapons').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Good Friday Agreement (1998).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. it established power-sharing arrangements in Northern Ireland through a new Assembly; it committed all parties to exclusively peaceful means of pursuing political change and received 71% support in a Northern Ireland referendum. Developing: identifies features without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Iraq War (2003) divided British political opinion more than any conflict since Suez.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers the scale of public opposition (c.1 million marching February 2003), the disputed WMD intelligence, the Chilcot Inquiry findings (decision taken before peaceful options exhausted, inadequate post-war planning), and the long-term political consequences (trust in political leaders). Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Troubles in Northern Ireland were difficult for successive British governments to resolve.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers deep historical roots (partition 1921), the complexity of the unionist and nationalist communities' conflicting aspirations, the IRA campaign and loyalist paramilitary violence, the damage done by events like Bloody Sunday to prospects for a political settlement, and the scale of compromise required in the Good Friday Agreement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did post-1945 conflicts change the relationship between the British state and its citizens? Explain your answer with reference to at least two conflicts.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers multiple dimensions of change (counter-terrorism legislation restricting civil liberties, Bloody Sunday and accountability of military force, Iraq War and limits of executive power in making war) and continuity (state security interests consistently prioritised, public protest generally contained rather than decisive); reaches a sustained evidenced judgement using at least two conflicts. Secure: Clear argument covering change and continuity across at least two conflicts. Developing: Mostly one conflict or one dimension. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Chilcot Inquiry's conclusions about the Iraq War (2003) were significant.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains what Chilcot concluded (WMD intelligence overstated, decision premature, post-war planning inadequate, legal basis unsatisfactory), why those conclusions mattered (accountability for flawed decision-making, implications for how Britain goes to war, public trust in government), and the significance of a public inquiry being able to reach such conclusions. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Linda Colley's argument about the origins of British identity.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Colley argued that British identity was 'forged' rather than natural (1); she dated the creation of Britishness to the eighteenth century, driven by shared Protestantism and war with France (1). Feature 2: Colley argued that before the Act of Union of 1707, 'Britain' barely existed as a meaningful identity (1); English, Scots, Welsh and Irish had separate identities, and Britishness was a political construction built on top of these (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the meaning of 'Britishness' changed significantly between 1948 and 1981.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons developed with evidence. Reason 1: The 1948 British Nationality Act defined Britishness broadly to include all Commonwealth subjects, expressing an imperial vision of a global British community; by 1981, this vision had been abandoned and the Act divided nationality into tiers based on ancestral connection to the UK. Reason 2: The arrival of Caribbean and South Asian migrants revealed that practical 'Britishness' was racialised — legal citizenship did not mean social acceptance; the hostility migrants faced showed that many people defined British identity in ethnic rather than civic terms. Secure: Both with evidence. Developing: One explained. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Stuart Hall argued that Black British identity was a 'hybrid' rather than simply Caribbean or simply British.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Hall's argument that diaspora identities are formed through the encounter between the migrant's cultural heritage and the culture of the host society; neither the original culture nor simple assimilation captures the lived experience; Black British culture created new forms (music, fashion, language, art) that drew on both traditions. Connects this to the political context of the 1970s-80s when Black British people faced racism and needed a positive identity that was neither rejection of Britishness nor denial of Caribbean heritage. Secure: Explains the hybrid concept with evidence. Developing: Describes Hall's ideas without full explanation. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which devolution changed the meaning of 'Britishness' after 1999.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Examples: devolution showed that Britishness was compatible with distinct national identities — one could be Scottish and British (1), as Scotland retained its own legal and educational system alongside Westminster membership (1); devolution created political institutions that expressed specifically Scottish and Welsh identities (1), meaning 'British' became a looser, multi-layered category than it had been under a unitary state (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the history of migration to Britain shows that 'Britishness' has always been defined by exclusion rather than inclusion? Use your knowledge of the whole period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that identifies both exclusion (Edict of Expulsion 1290 targeting Jews; Aliens Act 1905; 1962 and 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Acts; 1981 Nationality Act; 1919 race riots) and inclusion (Huguenot naturalisation; Polish Resettlement Act; 1948 Act's broad citizenship; Race Relations Acts; Parekh Report's civic model). Argues that the balance between exclusion and inclusion has shifted over time and has never been uniform — reception depended on race, religion, economic context and political circumstance. Engages with Linda Colley, Stuart Hall or Bhikhu Parekh. Secure: Clear argument with evidence across multiple periods. Developing: Some comparative points with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the idea of 'integration' (as defined by Roy Jenkins) differed from the idea of 'assimilation'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two differences explained causally. Difference 1: Assimilation required migrants to abandon their distinct cultural identity and adopt the majority culture; Jenkins's integration model preserved cultural diversity alongside civic participation.
