Difference 2: Assimilation assumed a single dominant culture that migrants must conform to; integration assumed a shared civic framework (equal opportunity, democratic values) within which multiple cultures could coexist — this underpinned the Parekh Report's 'community of communities' model. Secure: Two differences explained. Developing: One difference explained. Emerging: General statements.

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why the USA became involved in Vietnam between 1954 and 1965.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed reasons, each with specific detail (e.g. domino theory and Eisenhower's advisers; Gulf of Tonkin Resolution granting LBJ authority). Secure: Two identified reasons with some development. Developing: Two reasons identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution for US involvement in Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed consequences with specific evidence (authority to escalate without war declaration; Operation Rolling Thunder; first combat troops March 1965). Secure: Two consequences with supporting detail. Developing: Two consequences identified but development is limited. Emerging: One basic point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the USA failed to prevent the growth of the National Liberation Front in South Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation with multiple causal factors (Diem's unpopularity; refusal to hold 1956 elections; NLF land reform appeal) with specific detail and causal links. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Some explanation but limited detail. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the domino theory as used to justify US involvement in Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific detail (e.g. Eisenhower articulated it April 1954; it argued communist takeover in one state would trigger neighbours to fall). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why US involvement in Vietnam escalated from advisers to combat troops between 1954 and 1965.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes (domino theory; Diem's collapse; Gulf of Tonkin; NLF strength) with causal analysis and specific detail. Secure: Two causes developed with relevant evidence. Developing: One cause well-developed or two causes briefly stated. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Geneva Accords of 1954 failed to produce a lasting peace settlement in Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of multiple factors (failure to hold 1956 elections; NLF insurgency; US backing for Diem) linked coherently. Secure: Clear explanation with evidence. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Pipe Rolls are useful to historians studying Kenilworth Castle.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. they give exact sums spent on building and repair, so work can be dated and priced; they run in an unbroken series from the 1130s, so spending at Kenilworth can be traced reign by reign. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why churchwardens' accounts are valuable evidence about the Reformation in the parishes.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. they record what a parish actually paid for, such as a new Prayer Book, whitewash or the sale of vestments, so change can be tracked year by year; they were written for the parish itself, not for the government, so they show what really happened locally. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Compare what the Valor Ecclesiasticus and the reports of Cromwell's visitors suggest about the monasteries in 1535. Explain why they give different impressions.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: says what each source offers (income recorded house by house; charges of immorality and mismanagement), explains the difference from purpose and method (a careful financial survey against fast visits by men briefed to find fault), and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: both compared with some explanation. Developing: some comparison. Emerging: describes each separately.

practice_questions.text: Compare what Dugdale's 1656 Antiquities of Warwickshire and modern English Heritage interpretation panels suggest about Kenilworth Castle's significance. What do they reveal about how the castle has been understood at different times?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies agreement (both recognise site's historical importance) and difference (Dugdale writes shortly after slighting with royalist grief; English Heritage prioritises heritage tourism and contemporary accessibility); explains these differences using authorial context; supported conclusion. Secure: Similarities and differences with some contextual explanation. Developing: Some comparison. Emerging: Describes each source separately.

practice_questions.text: Explain why historians need more than one type of evidence to understand Kenilworth Castle.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: two developed reasons, e.g. royal accounts record what the Crown spent but never how servants lived, so household records and the fabric must fill the gap; the Great Mere no longer exists, so maps, engravings and archaeological survey are the only way to see it. Secure: two reasons with relevant detail. Developing: one reason developed. Emerging: simple statements.

practice_questions.text: Compare what a Pipe Roll entry and Dugdale's 1656 engravings of Kenilworth suggest about the castle. Explain what each can and cannot tell you.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 10 marks. Mastering: says what each shows (a Pipe Roll gives the cost and the year of a piece of royal building work; Dugdale gives the shape of the ruins soon after the slighting), explains that one is a record of money and the other a picture made by a royalist antiquary, and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: both compared with some explanation. Developing: some comparison. Emerging: describes each separately.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the devolution settlement established in Scotland in 1999.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. the Scottish Parliament could pass primary legislation on devolved matters including health, education and justice) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. it also had tax-varying powers — the ability to raise or lower income tax by up to 3p in the pound, giving it greater fiscal autonomy than any previous devolved body). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to Scotland having its own parliament. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 2010 coalition government.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. the coalition was formed after the 2010 election produced a hung Parliament — no party had an overall majority, requiring Conservative and Liberal Democrat leaders David Cameron and Nick Clegg to negotiate a formal agreement to govern together; the coalition agreed to raise university tuition fees to £9,000, breaking a prominent Liberal Democrat manifesto pledge — this caused the Liberal Democrats to lose 49 of 57 seats in 2015). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: vague reference to coalition government.

practice_questions.text: Explain why devolution in 1999 was a significant change in where power lay in the United Kingdom.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (the Scottish Parliament had primary legislative powers over health, education and justice — areas that directly affected millions of citizens, meaning decisions that previously required Westminster approval were now taken in Edinburgh; the creation of devolved bodies challenged the traditional doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty by giving legislative power to regional institutions for the first time since the Act of Union 1707; the close Welsh result (50.3%) showed uneven support but Blair's government proceeded — Westminster decided how much power to devolve rather than the regions themselves, showing limits to the change). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes devolution without explaining why it was significant.

practice_questions.text: Explain why coalition government created challenges for democratic accountability.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (neither party could implement its full manifesto — voters could not hold the government accountable for promises broken through compromise rather than political failure; the tuition fees example showed a specific manifesto promise (Liberal Democrat pledge to abolish fees) broken as a condition of coalition — the Liberal Democrats suffered massive electoral punishment in 2015 as a result; coalition agreements are negotiated after the election, not voted on — critics argued this gave unelected negotiators power to determine policy; voters choosing one party could end up being governed partly by another's programme). Secure: two factors with relevant evidence. Developing: describes the difficulties of coalition without explaining why they raised accountability problems. Emerging: vague reference to parties disagreeing.

practice_questions.text: How far did devolution and the events of 1997-2014 represent a fundamental change in where power lay in Britain? [You may consider: the 1997 referendums; the Scottish Parliament; the Good Friday Agreement; the 2014 referendum; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both the scale of change (Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly with genuine legislative powers; Good Friday Agreement — power-sharing in Northern Ireland; 2014 referendum showed 44.7% of Scots wanted independence, reflecting deep dissatisfaction with Westminster) and continuity (Westminster remained sovereign — it could repeal devolution Acts; the 2014 result preserved the Union; coalition government showed Parliament still functioned normally; English law and most taxation remained at Westminster). Overall judgement on whether 'fundamental change' is the right description. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes devolution accurately but does not weigh the extent of change. Emerging: narrative without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the key facts about the 2014 Scottish independence referendum.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific, accurate points (held on 18 September 2014; result was 55.3% No, 44.7% Yes; turnout was 84.6% — the highest in any UK election or referendum since universal suffrage; led by SNP's Alex Salmond (Yes) and Better Together campaign (No); Better Together included Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat politicians; Scotland remained in the United Kingdom). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Scotland voting to stay in the UK.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Thomason Tracts are useful to historians of the Civil War period.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. the collection holds about 22,000 printed items from 1640-1661, and George Thomason often dated each one as he bought it, so historians can track how print responded to events. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why royal proclamations are useful but limited as sources for the Personal Rule.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons, e.g. proclamations were the King's main way of issuing orders while Parliament was not sitting, so they show royal intent directly; but they do not show whether the orders were obeyed, so a ship money proclamation cannot tell you how much was collected. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain what the physical remains of Kenilworth Castle show about the impact of the Civil War on the site.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains two or more features (cut walls, roofless buildings, absent mere) as direct evidence of the 1649-50 slighting, and explains what physical evidence alone cannot show (motivations, broader political context). Notes the need for documentary evidence alongside physical remains. Secure: Two features linked to slighting with some evaluation. Developing: Describes features but limited evaluation. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: How far do royal proclamations and parliamentary diaries reveal opposition to Charles I? Use the sources and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates both sources on origin, purpose and content. Royal proclamation: shows royal intent, printed for distribution, not designed to reveal opposition. Parliamentary diary: gives texture of debate, but reflects one MP's perspective, may be selective. Explains what each is useful for and where each falls short. Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Compares both with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes one source more than comparing. Emerging: Mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Civil War pamphlets are useful to historians of radical politics in the 1640s.
practice_questions.marks: Ten marks are available. Mastering: two or more developed reasons with precise detail, e.g. pamphlets survive in huge numbers after censorship collapsed, they carry Leveller petitions and other radical demands in their own words, but they were written to persuade and are often anonymous. Secure: one reason explained with detail. Developing: a reason identified. Emerging: a simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why English Heritage interpretation at Kenilworth Castle is both useful and limited for historians studying the Civil War period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains why English Heritage is useful (synthesises scholarship, makes site accessible, uses physical and documentary evidence) and limited (secondary source, simplified, reflects current consensus that may change, audience is visitors not specialists). Uses specific reference to site interpretation. Secure: Two reasons for useful and limited. Developing: One point each way. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the Vietcong used guerrilla tactics against US forces in Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed ways, each with specific detail (e.g. tunnel systems at Cu Chi; ambushes and booby traps making enemy identification impossible). Secure: Two identified ways with some development. Developing: Two ways identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Tet Offensive of 1968 was a turning point in the Vietnam War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons with specific evidence (military failure of the offensive vs its psychological impact; LBJ's decision not to seek re-election; collapse of public confidence). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: Two reasons identified but development limited. Emerging: One basic reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain why opposition to the Vietnam War grew within the United States between 1968 and 1973.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation with multiple causal factors (Tet; My Lai; Kent State; Pentagon Papers; Cambodian invasion) linked coherently to the growth of opposition. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of Nixon's Vietnamisation policy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific detail (e.g. gradual US troop withdrawal from 543,000 in 1969; training South Vietnamese forces to take over combat). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why US tactics in Vietnam failed to defeat the Vietcong by 1968.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes (guerrilla tactics of the Vietcong; limitations of body count as measure of success; civilian casualties undermining US legitimacy) with causal analysis. Secure: Two causes with relevant evidence. Developing: One cause developed or two briefly stated. Emerging: Simple descriptive statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the My Lai massacre was significant for the Vietnam War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of its significance (escalation of domestic opposition; moral questions about free-fire zone policies; media reporting; credibility damage to the US government). Secure: Clear explanation with evidence. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Outline two consequences of the fall of Saigon in 1975 for the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed consequences with specific detail (e.g. 58,000 Americans dead; War Powers Act passed; damaged US credibility in Cold War). Secure: Two consequences with some development. Developing: Two consequences identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two features of the policy of détente in the period 1969–1979.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed features with specific evidence (SALT I 1972 freezing missile numbers; Nixon's 1972 China visit exploiting Sino-Soviet split; Helsinki Accords 1975). Secure: Two features with supporting detail. Developing: Two features identified but development limited. Emerging: One basic point.

practice_questions.text: Compare the orthodox and revisionist interpretations of the origins of the Cold War. How far do they differ, and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated comparison of named schools (orthodox, revisionist, post-revisionist) with named historians (Schlesinger, Williams, Gaddis), specific evidence for each, and an analysis of what changed each school's thinking. Secure: Clear comparison with named schools and some specific evidence. Developing: Two views identified but not developed as a comparative analysis. Emerging: Descriptive account of one viewpoint.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of SALT I signed in May 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific detail (e.g. froze numbers of ICBMs; first treaty to limit nuclear weapons growth). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the policy of détente broke down by 1979.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes (structural weakness of détente based on negotiation not shared values; Soviet invasion of Afghanistan December 1979; US withdrawal of SALT II) with causal analysis. Secure: Two causes with relevant evidence. Developing: One developed or two briefly stated. Emerging: Simple descriptive statement.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the USA was mainly responsible for the origins of the Cold War? Use your knowledge and the interpretations in this lesson to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument evaluating all three historical schools with named historians and specific evidence; weighs the revisionist claim against orthodox and post-revisionist counter-evidence; reaches a sustained and supported judgement. SPaG: accurate spelling and grammar, consistent use of historical terminology. Secure: Clear argument with named schools and evidence; judgement present but less fully developed. Developing: Some argument referencing two viewpoints; limited use of specific evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account of one viewpoint only.
